only Turkish the mass of information which previously had been
available only to the very few who had learned the languages of
the West.
  Diplomatic Missions. While the military teachers and their
presses provided important windows to the West for upper- and
lower-class Ottomans alike, the various channels of diplomacy
also made their contribution in this respect, although in a more
limited way. The principal agents of this sort of transmission
were the Sultan’s representatives sent to the important capitals \/
of Europe, and those of the various European powers stationed at
the Porte.
  Throughout the centuries of Ottoman greatness and decay, no
permanent Ottoman embassies were established in Europe since           V
it was felt that nothing could be learned from the infidels of the
West and that it was for the inferior monarchs of Europe to
petition for the Sultan’s favor through their representatives at
the Porte. Special Ottoman missions were sent to European
capitals but only for limited times to accomplish specific purposes,
principally to sign trade agreements and, more and more fre¬
quently during the eighteenth century, treaties of peace ceding
territories and making other concessions to the victorious powers
of Europe. In general the Ottomans who were sent on these
missions were neither qualified nor motivated to go beyond their
instructions and observe the lands through which they passed.
Only a few of them submitted any reports at all, and these for
the most part went little beyond descriptions of the ceremonials
and negotiations participated in during their trips. But there
were some exceptions.
  In 1664, Kara Mehmed Pasha, a member of the Bostanji corps,
was sent to Vienna with a suite of almost a hundred and fifty
persons, and his short description of that imperial capital was the




                        Window to the West
                                            i
                                      %




186   first work of any kind to give the leaders of the Porte a look at
      western life/ In 1720, Second Treasurer Ibrahim Pasha provided
      a similar short description of the same city on his return from
      negotiations there in coimection with the execution of the Treaty
      of Passarowitz/ In the same year, Yirmisekiz Chelebi Mehmed
      Faiz Efendi was sent to Paris as special Ottoman ambassador
      to the court of Louis XIV and, after a stay of two years, submitted
      to his master a long and detailed report, describing life not only
      in the French capital, but also in^ several other French cities
      which he visited, by far the most important and detailed report
      of this kind received by the Porte until the time of Selim III/
      In 1754 and again in 1764, the scribe of the Silahdar corps,
      Mehmed Dervish Efendi, was sent as Ottoman plenipotentiary to
      Saint Petersburg, and his reports gave a great deal of detail on
      the Russian modernization program then in progress/® Ahmed
      Resmi submitted two reports of this kind, one describing Vienna
      during his sojourn there in 1757-58 and the other depicting
      Berlin in great detail, as a result of his mission to the Prussian

        None of these reports are of great value by our standards;
      many of them are more interesting for what they did not include
      than for what they did. Yet they did provide the sultans and
      those around them with some notion of the technical and moral
      achievements of the West and they were, in the absence of
      anything better, means of making some breaks in the wall of
      Ottoman isolation. For the most part, however, the sultans had
      to rely on the European ambassadors and others resident in Istan-
      bul for regular reports of events and conditions in Europe. Since
      each ambassador naturally limited and distorted the news so as to
      favor the prestige and position of his own country, the sultans
      and their ministers remained by far the most poorly informed of
      any European rulers concerning events and conditions outside
      their own domains.
        By Selim’s time, the conditions which made possible such




                         The "New Order” of Selim III
ignorance were changing so rapidly that progress would probably          187
have been made even if the Sultan had not been especially eager
to learn about Europe. The Ottoman government was now be¬
coming intimately involved with European powers by military
alliance. It was seeking their technical and financial assistance
on a large scale. It was maneuvering for position among them.
This hardly fitted in with the old picture of a Porte content to
wait for foreigners to come and beg favors. The Porte now re¬
quired a knowledge of European affairs far more regular, de¬
tailed, and objective than that which seemingly had sufficed
before. When addgd to Selim’s desire to learn of European life
and technical accomplishments, reform of the Ottoman diplo¬
matic service was inevitable, and in 1793 it was decided to estab¬
lish permanent Ottoman legations in the important capitals of
Europe as soon as possible.
  It would seem that Paris should have been the most natural
choice for the first Ottoman embassy. Selim had always been
most favorable to France, and he hoped that it would provide
most of the technical assistance that he wanted. Europe was now
embroiled in the opening stages of the wars of the French Revolu¬
tion, however, and while Selim was most anxious to receive tech-     h
nicians from revolutionary France, he was quite unhappy about
the fate of the French king with whom he had corresponded so
hopefully only a few years before. Moreover France was in mortal
combat with most of the royal powers of Europe, who hoped to
stamp out the "contagion” of democracy before it could spread.
The new regime had been outlawed, and no one had yet officially
recognized it. An Ottoman embassy to Paris at this time would
most certainly have involved official recognition, and Selim did
not wish to recognize the new government until a precedent
had been established by another great European power. So
France was ignored at the start.Likewise Selim did not wish
to honor the court at Saint Petersburg with one of his represent-    ^
atives because of the bitterness engendered by the recent war
and various disputes which had arisen over the execution of the
Treaty of Jassy.

  Many of the European ambassadors resided in the Ottoman
Empire for years. They were acquainted with its languages and
customs, and cultivated close and lasting relationships with Otto¬
man officials, paying regular bribes in order to learn their policies
and decisions and to influence them when possible.^® As a result,
the reports they sent to Europe concerning internal Ottoman af¬
fairs give far more reliable and detailed information on Turkey
than do the Ottoman chronicles and governmental materials of
the time. At the same time, each European nation maintained its
own regular courier service to and from the Porte, sending news¬
papers and memoranda containing information and news, and
these were often passed on to Ottoman officials through various
channels, providing them with their only regular news of Europe.
  While Selim was still a prince in the palace of Abd ul-Hamid I,
his main source of contact with the outside world had been the
French ambassadors. After Selim’s accession, he continued to rely

European, often meeting him outside the Palace in disguise in
order to dispense with the formalities required by protocol.^^

lutionary government of France in October 1792 and fled to
Russia in exile two months later, leaving France without official

various ways to Ottoman awareness of the West.
  Of course all these diplomatic contacts had only a slight effect
on Ottoman society as a whole. Access to the reports sent from
Ottomans in Europe, as to the Europeans themselves at the Porte,
was limited to a very few Ottomans who were directly concerned
with foreign affairs. The knowledge imparted through these
sources was transmitted to other Ottomans only indirectly, if at
all. However, in the unofficial activities of the European repre¬
sentatives, merchants, and technicians now present in increasing
numbers in Istanbul, there was an impact which was much more
extensive and in the long run even more significant for the whole
of Ottoman society.


                        Social Contacts
  The time of the French Revolution saw a tremendous relaxa¬
tion in the social barriers which isolated the Europeans in the
Ottoman Empire from the Ottomans among whom they lived. In
previous centuries the few foreigners who did reside in the Sul¬
tan’s dominions isolated themselves almost entirely in their own
compounds. Mutual distrust and even hostility and scorn, com¬
bined with a more practical and justified European fear of con¬
tracting the plague then widespread in the empire, limited contact
to purely formal occasions. And even then most of the actual
intercourse was left to the mediation of translators serving both




                         Window to the West
194   sides, who used their positions to advance their own causes and
      interests at the expense of those whom they were supposed to he
      serving.
         But new developments during Selim’s reign made it impossible
      for this sort of isolation to continue. The very fact that foreign
      diplomats, merchants, and soldiers were living in Istanbul in
      far greater numbers than in earlier times made it inevitable that
      opportunities for contact would greatlyvincrease. Selim’s reforms
      and his efforts to popularize them w^hett6d the appetities of many
      Ottomans, at least to the extent of making them for the first time
      somewhat curious about the strange infidels in their midst and
      desirous of learning of their manners and ways. Moreover Euro¬
      peans long content to ignore the Ottomans in the past were now
      compelled by the need to compete for the favor of the neutral
      Porte to try to cultivate the friendship and understanding of all
      segments of the population.
        As a result of these factors, intercourse increased on all levels
      of society. European parties and entertainments held in the great
      embassy palaces and private homes were now attended by Otto¬
      man officials, including the Sultan himself in disguise. Upper-
      class Ottomans began to imitate the practices of European society
      and hold parties in their own homes and palaces, into which their
      European acquaintances were invited for the first time. Western
      merchants, technicians, and soldiers met subjects of the Sultan in
      the streets, bazaars, and coffeehouses. Street performances by
      European actors, buffoons, jugglers, and the like became regular
      features of lower-class Ottoman city life.^*^ The large cities of the
      empire witnessed a craze on the part of all classes of the popula¬
      tion for European clothing, architecture, and furniture, so much
      so that the British ambassador. Sir Robert Liston, reported in
      1796 that "the fashion of the day is strongly in favor of European
      imitation in every rank of society.”4*^ Selim himself is said to have
      invited European actors to perform in his palace, attempted imi¬
      tations of western music and poetry in his own compositions, and
      imported western flowers and miniature pictures for his personal
      use.^°
        These were the effects produced by Europeans of all nationali¬
      ties, but in addition the French had a special impact. Turkey at




                         The "New Order” of Selim III
this time was one of the few neutral countries in Europe, and it       195
therefore provided a unique place where friend and foe of the
Revolution could dwell in uncomfortable proximity. Exiled French
royalists lived side by side with the most ardent supporters of the
Revolution, and conflicts and competition were inevitable. The
Jacobins in Istanbul affixed revolutionary emblems to their per¬
sons and homes, held public ceremonies to celebrate the great
events of the Revolution, and did all they could to secure public
and private support for their' cause among Ottomans and foreign¬
ers alike. They went into the coffeehouses, spoke of the rights of
man and the evils of the old regime, and distributed Turkish- and
French-language leaflets and broadsheets expounding the ideas
of liberty, equality, and fraternity.^^ In many cases, they tried to
provoke riots among the volatile Istanbul mob as a means of
exerting pressure on the Turkish government to support the new
regime in France.In January 1793, they even went so far as to
plant a Tree of Liberty on a terrace in full view of the Sultan’s
palace!
  Much of this activity was inspired and directed locally by
Frenchmen in Istanbul wishing to show their loyalty to the new
regime. Some of it was directed by agents sent from France. Num¬
erous revolutionary societies and clubs were organized, of which
the most important were the Societe Republicaine des Amis de la
Liberie et de I’Egalite, established by Descorches in August,
1793,^^ and the Societe Populaire Republicaine, inaugurated by
Henin about the same time.^^ These, and others as well, occasion¬
ally cooperated, but more often they were as violently hostile to
one another on ideological and personal grounds as they were to
the royalists.Once the French government was officially recog¬
nized by the Porte and French ambassadors came from Paris to
occupy the palace of the embassy, these groups were directed on a
more centralized basis and their mutual hostility was curbed
although not entirely eliminated. The French embassy now also
took the main role in spreading revolutionary propaganda in the
empire. In April 1795, Louis Allier, director of the Imprimerie
Nationale in Paris, was sent to Istanbul with two new presses and
several assistants to reorganize and expand the small press pre¬
viously operated at the embassy there under Descorches’s aegis.^®

  During most of this time, the Ottoman government was trying
to maintain its neutrality among the warring European powers,
and this effort was reflected in its attitude to the revolutionary
and antirevolutionary activities and appeals. The Ottoman cabi¬
net itself was divided on what should be done. Kuchiik Hiiseyin
Pasha, the Treasurer Ibrahim Efendi, and Ebubekir Ratib Efendi
usually advocated a conciliatory policy toward the Jacobins,
while Mustafa Reshid and Yusuf Agah led those who favored the
British and royalist position.®® As a result, the Porte vacillated,
sometimes restricting the Jacobins and sometimes giving them
full freedom so that in the end they were able to continue their
work most of the time.^®
 There was also another channel through which revolutionary
doctrines entered the Ottoman Empire at this time. In Paris, the
documents of revolution were translated into Serbian, Greek, and
Armenian, as well as into Turkish, and these were disseminated
widely in the European portions of the empire and the Mediter¬
ranean islands. Even in times of closest French cooperation with
the Porte, French agents were sent to Ali Pasha of Janina, to
Dalmatia, to Serbia, Greece, Crete, and Cyprus, preaching the
advantages of republicanism and liberty and trying to make

198   certain that if the Porte did choose to side with the enemies of the

      strongly by Ottoman, British, and Russian agents, were quite

      and the Sultan. Selim himself had a German and an Italian doc¬

      late his taste for it.^^ There were European women in the harem
      of the Sultan, and they are reputed to have provided important
      channels of contact between the Palace and the West. Also the
      Jews of the empire as well as Greek and Armenian merchants
      and aristocrats long had been in intimate contact with relatives,
      friends, and business associates living in the various countries of
      Europe. Through private correspondence, they were in constant
      touch with Europe, and it must be assumed that they passed on
      at least a certain amount of the information derived to their
      Ottoman associates. The most direct means by which this sort of
      information was communicated to the Porte was through the
      office of Bash Terjuman, the chief translator of the Imperial Coun¬
      cil and official in charge of relations with foreign representatives.^^
      After the late seventeenth century, this important position was
      held exclusively by members of the wealthy Greek Phanariote
      families of Istanbul, who kept it just because their contacts with
      the West made them more knowledgeable of Europe than their
      Ottoman brothers.^^ In addition, these and other Greek and Ar¬
      menian families often sent their children to be educated in Europe,
      in Italy in particular, thus preparing them both linguistically
      and intellectually to receive the new western ideas of their time
      and to transmit them to the Ottomans at the Porte.^^
        It is difficult to assess the extent to which these Western in¬
      fluences and ideas took root among the Ottomans of Selim’s time.
      The fact that he and those around him did try to imitate Europe
      in some respects, and the certainty that their efforts had some




                          The "New Order" of Selim III
support among rulers and subjects alike, would seem to indicate        199
that there was at least some effect. Yet this should not be over¬
stressed. As we have seen, most of the "reforms” were in fact
traditional Ottoman responses to the needs of the time, and the
relative ease with which Selim was deposed in 1807 indicates his
lack of deep-seated support among rulers and subjects alike.
That the Sultan himself retained in essence the spirit and men¬
tality of the past is demonstrated further by the nature of the
literary efforts which were supported in his court. With the doc¬
trines of revolution swirling around him, Sultan Selim chose to
promote the efforts' of poets and writers who reflected only the
themes and values of the past. Thus the great writers of the French
Revolutionary era in Istanbul were the Mevlevi leader Sheyh
Galib (1757-1799) and his brother dervishes at the Galata monas¬
tery, Hulusi Dede (d. 1805) and Esrar Dede (d. 1797) as well as
Seyyid Vehbi (d. 1809) and the great Fazil Bey (d. 1808), who rep¬
resented the last great flourish of the traditional Ottoman literary
schools. For them, as for their patron, it was the empty, mystical
searchings for the supreme being and the never-ending descrip¬
tions of court frivolities that excited attention rather than the
political, social, and economic problems of their time. That no
modern school of literature appeared in Selim’s time seems to
be clear evidence that the ideas of the West, however freely they
came into the capital, took no root but at best left the seeds for
a flowering which was to come only under Selim s successors.^®

Part IV. Disintegration of the Empire:
 Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars,
             1792-1807
           XV. Disintegration of the
             Empire, 1792-1798




                   /




The Treaty of Jassy left Selim III relatively free from foreign
dangers for almost six years, yet even then his efforts to take ad¬
vantage of this respite to strengthen the empire by internal re¬
forms were for the most part frustrated by the need to undertake
regular campaigns against revolts which sprang up everywhere V
in his empire. These uprisings diverted more and more of his
energy and resources and at the same time sapped the strength
and vitality of the central government.
  Internal disintegration certainly was not a problem unique
Selim’s age. One of the earliest evidences of Ottoman decline —
even in the sixteenth century—had been the central government’s
increasing inability to enforce its will in the provinces. Incompe¬
tent, tyrannical, and dishonest officials, and economic and social
chaos led to the rise of numerous separatist movements, them¬
selves both causes and manifestations of the decline.
  The notables were responsible for one kind of revolt. Individ- /
uals and families who were locally prominent because of wealth
or religious and social prestige had come to occupy influential
places in their communities. They were called notables (ayan) ]C
and were looked to as arbiters and leaders by those around them.
Because of their influence with the people, they were increasingly
consulted and used by Ottoman officials to secure local compliance
        with their orders and desires. During the eighteenth century
 ^      their positions often became hereditary. They assumed the func-
        tion of mediating between the people and the government officials
        and, as the latter became more corrupt and tyrannical, of inter¬
        vening to protect the people from the officials. And finally, as the
        officials no longer were able or willing to carry out the duties of
        government, these notables stepped in to take over police duties,
        apportion and collect taxes, organize irrigation and cultivation,
        arrange for the supply of food an^ otlier necessities, and even
       provide soldiers and military provisions for the Imperial army.
       They thus became the principal administrators of local govern¬
       ment and the defenders of their communities against the worst
       excesses of the increasingly incompetent and dishonest officials
       sent from Istanbul. The Ottoman government began to recognize
       them officially in an effort to exercise some supervision and con¬
       trol over them, but for the most part they continued to be chosen
       locally and to operate in almost complete independence.
         At the same time, cultivators and townfolk driven from their
       homes by vexation, oppression, and insecurity, soldiers fleeing
       from the tyranny and incompetence of their officers as well as
       from defeats at the hands of superior enemies, and tribesmen and
       mountain dwellers, ever willing to oppose settled authority, came
      / together with the worst elements of the population to form bandit
y I    armies which devastated the length and breadth of the empire,
       from the mountains of Bosnia to the valleys of the Tigris and the
       Nile. In the absence of effective government opposition, many of
       them came to control whole districts and even provinces, and
     .^(Aheir chiefs, known in some places as Derebeys (Lords of the Val¬
       ley), made themselves almost entirely independent of central
       control, while the government officials supposed to administer
       their areas became little more than ambassadors to their courts.
       Usually called mountain brigands and usurpers by the Ottoman
       chroniclers of the time, they became for all practical purposes
       vassal princes, maintaining autonomous powers over large areas
       with only minimal acknowledgement of the suzerainty of the
       Sultan. As they came to control the large towns in their areas,
       there was little to distinguish them from the local notables, who
       in many cases led, or at least encouraged, supplied, and used
       them.



                        Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
  Some of these Derebeys and notables were closely related to         213
local families and identified the prosperity and security of the 1/
area with their own self-interest. Within limits, such leaders did
a good deal to develop and restore agriculture, trade, and industry
and to protect their holdings against the attacks of rivals. Since
most of them maintained their positions for long periods of time,
they were able to consider the long-term interests of the lands
which they ruled to a far greater extent than could the Ottoman
officials who had to use their relatively short terms mainly to
raise money to pay off the bribes they were forced to pay in order
to secure and keep^their positions. Often the rule of the notables
was therefore preferred by local inhabitants to an3dhing govern- y'
ment officials could accomplish.
  In addition since the military corps, which traditionally pro¬
vided men for the regular Ottoman army, had become disorgan¬
ized and incapable of carrying out their military functions, the ^
Porte was forced to rely more and more on these local leaders for
men to fight its wars. They in turn used these military activities
to increase their own power, by taking vast amounts of booty
from Ottoman and enemy populations alike and by absorbing into
their own armies many of the enemy troops as well as the regular
Ottoman soldiers with whom they served. So in the end, they re¬
turned to their homes with far more powerful forces than when
they departed, leaving the Porte increasingly unable to suppress
their independence.
  In fact by Selim’s time the Porte had little desire to suppress
them, even if it had the ability to do so. The regularity and size
of their tribute and tax payments and the effectiveness of their
military contingents contrasted quite favorably with those from
areas under direct Ottoman rule. Moreover these notables and
Derebeys were able to create, in the capital, political parties
favorable to their interests by providing regular subsidies to
influential persons who did all they could to prevent or frustrate
actions against their patrons.
  The most that the Porte did, or tried to do, was to keep the
loyalty and friendship of the predominant notables to retain the
tribute and military assistance which they provided. This was
accomplished by various means. For one thing, the Porte was well
aware of the fact that the degree to which these notables con-



               Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
214    tinued to accept Ottoman suzerainty and to carry out their ob¬
       ligations varied in direct relation to the extent of local opposition
       they had to face. Those who had to fight the attacks of relatively
       equal opponents were quite willing to accept whatever assistance
       the Ottoman officials could give them and to honor their obliga¬
       tions to the Porte in return. When they were able to rid them¬
       selves of their principal competitors, Ottoman control and influ¬
       ence declined accordingly. A major task for the Ottoman officials
      ^ therefore was to keep the conflicting local notables and factions
       equally matched so that all would continue to seek Ottoman
       support and perform their obligations in return. It was only when
       local notables obtained absolute, uncontested power in their
       areas and disregarded their tribute and^ military contributions
       to the Porte that efforts were made to control them by more force¬
       ful means.
         Another means by which the notables were kept loyal to the
       Ottoman cause was by their appointment to official ranks and
       positions, including that of governor in the districts which they
       dominated. In many cases, where military dangers became press¬
       ing, important notables were actually appointed as military
       commanders (serasker) of the Ottoman army on the fronts where
       their forces were needed and used. Under these circumstances,
       the Porte lost its ability to play off, control, and use local factions,
       and its long-range ability to maintain its position and fulfill its
       desires declined accordingly.*
         In the age of the French Revolution, there were innumerable
       "despots,” "tyrants,” and "rebels” operating all over the empire.
       Their constant raids as well as their struggles among themselves
       and with Ottoman expeditionary forces fill large sections of the
       chronicles of the time. To enumerate and describe them all would
       be a complicated, unending, and fruitless task, yet to leave the
       subject without discussing the most important of them would be
       to ignore an essential portion of Ottoman history at that time.

                     The Arab Provinces
  In Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Arabia, Ottoman weakness also left
political vacuums, but these were filled less by local movements
with popular support than they were by Ottoman officials and
Mamluk and bedouin chiefs' who sought to seize power for their
own benefit. The Arabic-speaking natives were no more than pas¬
sive observers of their struggles, neither participating in nor
benefiting from them.
  During the last half of the seventeenth century, power in Otto¬
man Egypt gradually fell from the hands of Ottoman officials,
who composed the official hierarchy of government, to their Mam¬
luk slaves, who gained their freedom and rose to be rulers and
masters. By 1671, the transition from Ottoman to Mamluk con¬
trol was largely complete, with most of the administrative and
military positions being filled by members of the Mamluk fac¬
tions, the leader of the most important of these acting as the real
ruler of the country with the title Sheyh ul-Beled or "chief of the
city.” Only the position of governor (vali) continued to be filled by
vezirs appointed from Istanbul. While these governors relin¬
quished most of their administrative functions to the Sheyh ul-
Beled, they continued to perform an important role by playing
off the various Mamluk factions against one another and keeping
them relatively equal so that they were eager and willing to rec¬
ognize the Sultan’s suzerainty and to pay the taxes and tribute he
demanded in return for his support. So long as the governors were
able to maintain such a balance, the Ottoman treasury secured
sufficient revenues to fulfill its financial needs in Egypt, and was
content to leave the actual functioning of the government in the
hands of the Mamluks. But after 1779, Egypt fell under the con¬
trol of a Mamluk coalition led by Murad and Ibrahim Beys, who
ruled almost continuously for the rest of the century. For a time
they continued to pay their taxes and tribute. But once they had
eliminated their rivals and established virtually unopposed rule
after 1783, they reduced and largely ended their payments. Only




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
218   then did the Porte send a military expedition to curb them, under
      the leadership of the Grand Admiral) Gazi Hasan Pasha (1786).
      His object was not to restore direct Ottoman administration since
      he was well aware that the Porte would lack the power to enforce
      such a position once his expeditionary force returned to Istanbul.
      Rather he sought only to restore the various Mamluk factions so
      they would be able to administer the country while paying for the
      governor’s encouragement and support.' Since the outbreak of a
      new war with Russia (1787) forced Gazi Hasan to leave before he
      could bring about a satisfactory solution, it was not long before
      Murad and Ibrahim returned to power. As a result of Hasan’s
      work in building up the other Mamluk factions, however, Murad
      and Ibrahim never were able to eliminate their rivals entirely
      thereafter, and they remained sufficiently dependent on the Porte
      to be forced to pay taxes and tribute although at an ever-decreas¬
      ing rate.
        As a result of this rivalry, during the last quarter of the eight¬
      eenth century there were constant struggles among the various
      Mamluk factions, with Murad and Ibrahim never being able to
      achieve sufficient strength to overcome them and establish rela¬
      tive calm. Each faction ravaged town and country alike to finance
      its efforts, and none of them had the ability or time to perform the
      duties of police and administration needed to keep order and se¬
      curity in the land. Consequently by 1798 Egypt was in political,
      economic, and social chaos. The depredations of Mamluk and
      bedouin bands, the disintegration of the irrigation system, and
      the ravages of plague rapidly depopulated the country and left it
      an easy prey to whoever chose to attack it from outside.^
        In Syria the outstanding Mamluk leader of Selim Ill’s time was
      Ahmed Jezzar Pasha. Originally a Bosnian, he entered Ottoman
      service in the household of Hekimoglu Ali Pasha and in 1756
      accompanied his master to Egypt, where he was appointed gov¬
      ernor. When Ali returned to Istanbul at the end of his term,
      Ahmed managed to remain in Cairo and soon allied himself with
      the famous Ali Bey al-Kabir, first as the slave of one of All’s
      Mamluks and later as a Mamluk of Ali himself. It was during this
      period that Ahmed acquired the nickname of Jezzar (the butcher)
      as the result of his ferocious efforts in the internecine Mamluk

struggles for power and in the suppression of the hedouins in the      219
Delta.«
  Ahmed quarreled with Ali’s chief lieutenant, Abu al-Zahab,
and was forced to flee from Egypt in 1769. For a time he served
the Ottoman governor of Damascus against the rebel riojer of
Acre, Zahir al-Omar. During these campaigns, Ahmed won the
attention and favor of Gazi Hasan Pasha, and as a result he him¬
self was appointed governor of Acre (1775). At this time he sup¬
pressed the rebellions of Zahir’s sons and the efforts of the bed¬
ouin tribes to ravage the agricultural areas. As reward he was
made leader of theXlttoman pilgrims’ caravan to the Holy Cities
(1770) and then governor of Sidon (1775) and later of Damascus
as well (1785).Ahmed now attracted into his service large num¬
bers of Bosnians and Albanians left in Syria by the Ottoman
armies, and he soon built them into the strongest army in the
area. With his base continuing at Acre, he expanded his authority
and influence throughout much of Syria, Lebanon, and Palestine.
Local ruling families had to accept his authority both as Ottoman
governor and local notable, and they paid tribute in return for
his "protection.” With these revenues, he not only paid all the
taxes he owed to the Sultan, but also enlarged his army, built a
small navy, and so extended his power that he was by far the
strongest ruler in Syria during the last quarter of the century.
  The only successful opposition which he met came from Mount
Lebanon and in particular from the Shihabi Emir Bashir II, who
was first chosen as governor of the Lebanon by its leading fami¬
lies in 1789. Bashir actually was given power by the Janbulat
chiefs with the assistance of Jezzar’s soldiers, but Bashir success¬
fully countered Jezzar’s efforts to extend his power into the moun¬
tain. Despite his ostensible submission, he gradually built up his
own power in the Lebanon by playing off the various families
against one another and gradually confiscating their properties
for his own benefit. As a result, by the end of the century he was a
powerful rival.
  Ottoman authority also began to wane in Iraq in the last years
of the seventeenth century. For over a half century thereafter
struggles for power continued without end, with the bedouins
ravaging the countryside and the province falling into political.




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
220   economic, and social chaos. It was only in the middle of the eight¬
      eenth century that the vacuum was at last filled hy the Mamluk
      slaves brought in to serve the Ottoman officials in the same way
      as they had in Egypt. But unlike the Egyptian example, once the
      Mamluks gained control in Iraq, they filled all the offices in the
      Ottoman hierarchy of government, including the governorship,
      which came to he held hy the chief of the dominant party. For
      this reason, the Porte never was abld to maintain competing
      Mamluk factions for its own benefit', and the Sultan’s treasury
      therefore never secured the same sort of financial reward as it
      had from Egypt. While the Iraqi Mamluks did divide into compet¬
      ing factions, there was always one which was able to achieve
      unchallenged control for long periods of,time. With the fear of
      oppression removed, their rulers were far freer to develop the
      security and prosperity of the country and to restore its adminis¬
      tration than the Mamluks were in Egypt.”
        This trend culminated under the greatest of the Mamluk rulers
      of Iraq, Suleyman Pasha "The Great,” whose period of enlight¬
      ened rule (1780-1802) largely coincided with that of Selim III.
      When Suleyman came to power, he found that the interregnum
      following the death of his predecessor, Umar Pasha (1764-1780),
      had been used by the bedouins of the Middle Euphrates, Arabia,
      and Syria, to ravage the countryside and defy the authority of the
      central government. At the same time, local rulers had declared
      their independence in the north at Mosul and Mardin and in the
      south at Basra, withholding the tax revenues of their areas for
      their own treasuries. To meet these challenges, Suleyman first
      had to establish his position in Baghdad itself. By restoring order
      and security in the capital, he gained the support of the local
      merchants, whose businesses had been ruined by the previous
      disorder. At the same time he found the long-established Janis¬
      sary corps to be as disorganized and ill-fitted for fighting as were
      their namesakes in Istanbul, while the Mamluks were dispirited
      and reduced in numbers as a result of the long years of factional
      disputes. Suleyman decided to rebuild the Mamluk forces to pro¬
      vide the base for his power. To do this he imported large numbers
      of slaves from Georgia and quickly trained them into an effective
      fighting force. He then appointed the best of them as officers in




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
the Janissary corps, and used the Mamluk army to force the Jan¬        221
issaries to accept discipline, training, and new weapons. So with¬
in a short time, he created an effective fighting force for himself.
  Once this was accomplished, Suleyman moved to restore order
in the countryside. He sent out regular expeditions which re¬
moved the bedouin tribes from the cultivated areas and forced
them to perform in his service, both to guard caravans and boats
and to serve in his armies against those of their fellows who had
not yet accepted his rule. The river and road bandits were almost
entirely eliminated, and once again the Tigris and Euphrates
were open for communications. Some of the stronger bedouin
tribes managed to retain their independence, however, and they
periodically threw off Suleyman’s domination and carried out
raids as far as Baghdad itself The leader of this opposition was
Sheyh Thuwaini, leader of the Muntafik tribe of Suk ul-Shuyuh,
who had attracted large numbers of bedouins and Mamluks who
refused to accept Suleyman’s domination. In 1784, Thuwaini
captured Zubair and Basra, arrested Suleyman’s officials, and
forced the local notables to petition the Sultan to appoint him to
Suleyman’s place in Baghdad. To combat this move, Suleyman got
the support of Thuwaini’s rival among the Muntafik, Hamid
al-Thamir, who gathered the bedouins of the Middle Euphrates
and some Kurdish tribes from the north. The combined govern¬
ment-bedouin force smashed Thuwaini at Umm ul-Abbas (Octo¬
ber 1787). Hamud now was appointed in place of his rival as
chief of the Muntafik, and Suleyman re-established his direct
authority in Basra.Thuwaini managed to escape capture and
took refuge in Arabia, where the rising Wahhabi movement
based its power. With Thuwaini’s encouragement, the Wahhabis
turned their attention to Iraq, and their raids in subsequent
years came to occupy most of Suleyman’s attention.
  In Arabia revolt against Ottoman rule during the late eight¬
eenth and early nineteenth centuries was focused in the activi¬
ties of the Wahhabi religious movement and the armies of the
Saudi family, who first rose to power in the middle of the eight¬
eenth century. The founder of the Wahhabis, Muhammad ibn
Abd al-Wahhab, was born in 1703 at Ayaina, near Riyadh. He
was the son of an extremely pious local judge who bitterly op-




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
222   posed the way in which his religion, as it was practiced in central
      Arabia at that time, had become a cult of superstitious beliefs
      in the efficacy of sacrifices, charms, and visitations to holy places,
      very much like the primitive religions which had existed in Arabia
      in the "age of ignorance” preceding the rise of Islam in the sev¬
      enth century. Muhammad accepted the teachings of his father;
      and after traveling to the Holy Cities and Basra for study, he
      began to preach a message of moral and spiritual regeneration,
      abandonment of idolatrous practiceis,' and return to the original
      religion of the Prophet. As soon as he attracted some followers,
      however, he encountered the opposition of local merchants whose
      businesses benefited from the traffic stimulated by the worship
      of saints and pilgrimages to holy places. They finally forced him
      to leave and return home, where he remained in study and medi¬
      tation until his father’s death in 1740.
        It was at this point that Muhammad moved to spread his mes¬
      sage by allying himself with local civil rulers and working with
      them for mutual advantage. In Ayaina he married the daughter
      of the local ruler, Uthman ibn Muammar, who gave him political
      support for his campaign for the first time. Under Muhammad’s
      spiritual direction and with Uthman’s army, Ayaina was trans¬
      formed into a model Muslim community of the type they hoped
      to spread to all of Arabia. Trees, saints’ tombs, and other objects
      venerated by the ignorant were destroyed; vice was eliminated;
      adulterous women were stoned to death; all opposition was vig¬
      orously suppressed. But Muhammad soon met the same sort of
      opposition he had encountered earlier in the Holy Cities. Not
      only did the populace object to interference in their lives, but the
      local merchants also felt the loss of revenues from the pilgrims’
      traffic, and they finally forced Uthman to get rid of him in 1745.
        Muhammad then moved to the nearby town of Dariye, where he
      rapidly built up a new circle of persons devoted to his message.
      It was not long before he came into contact with the ruler of nearby
      Turaif, Muhammad ibn Saud, who saw in the Wahhabi message
      an opportunity to spread his political rule in the area. Once again,
      Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab allied himself with a political
      ruler for mutual advantage. He provided Saud with a doctrine to
      attract supporters and followers while Saud gave him the finan-




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
cial and military support and protection needed to spread and         223
enforce his teachings.
  Dari ye now became the center of the Wahhabi moral and spir¬
itual revival movement. People flocked to hear Muhammad ibn
al-Wahhab’s teachings, coming not only from the immediate
vicinity, but from all over Arabia, so the movement soon ceased
to have a merely local character. Muhammad expanded his mes¬
sage to include the idea of holy war against enemies of Islam,
including all Muslims who were not true to their faith, that is,
everyone who refused to accept his teachings, with one-fifth of
the booty from su9h wars reserved for prince and preacher to
assure the strength and vitality of both civil and religious as¬
pects of the alliance. The wealth and manpower coming through
the Wahhabi movement enabled Ibn Saud to eliminate his princi¬
pal enemies in the Nejd by 1758. With his death in 1765, the first
stage in the rise and expansion of the Wahhabi-Saudi state was
brought to an end.*^
  Abd ul-Aziz I Ibn Saud had assumed actual political and mili¬
tary leadership of the state some time before his father’s death,
so there was no problem or dispute over succession. The bedouin
tribes which had declared allegiance to his father did not hesi¬
tate to transfer their support. It was under Abd ul-Aziz that the
state founded by his father expanded out of the Nejd to rule most
of Arabia and in fact to threaten the foundations of the Ottoman
Empire. Abd ul-Aziz first continued his father’s policy of consoli¬
dating his power in the Nejd by pushing his suzerainty to oasis
after oasis and tribe after tribe, each of which accepted the Wah¬
habi teachings, at least formally, as part of the price of submis¬
sion. The Nejd now began to suffer from drought and locusts, so
to find food and fodder for his followers and their animals, in
1769 Abd ul-Aziz inaugurated a series of raids into southern
Iraq. The raids were successful, and he acquired more and more
support among tribes not only in the Nejd but also in the Hijaz
and along the coasts of the Persian Gulf. As the political succes¬
ses mounted, the religious message became more specific. To the
followers of the Wahhabi message, all the rituals of religion had
to be obeyed to the letter as manifestations of sincere belief, and
all aberrations, including failure to pray even a single time, were




              Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
224   considered to be the worst sort of sin, punishable by death. To sins
      such as the construction of tombs, lighting of candles, and venera¬
      tion and worship of saints and prophets were added the use of
      drink and tobacco and the playing of music, which were considered
      to be heretical innovations since they were not specifically men¬
      tioned in the Koran. All Muslims who had not yet accepted the
      Wahhabi teachings were considered to be pagans or polytheists
      who had to be converted or killed. To be sure, this doctrine alone
      could not have attracted the sincere support of the free-living
      townsmen and tribesmen of Arabia, but the political and military
      success that went with it, and in particular the possibility of
      acquiring large amounts of booty, seemed to be worth the price
      of accepting at least formally the doctrines which accompanied
      them.*®
        At this time, Ottoman rule in Arabia was concentrated at a few
      forts located along the Red Sea coast as stations for the annual
      pilgrimages to the Holy Cities, the ports of Yanbo and Jidda and
      tbe Holy Cities themselves. All of these were under the governor¬
      ship of the Sherif of Mecca, who, in addition to being the repre¬
      sentative of the Sultan, was accepted as suzerain by most of the
      bedouin tribes who lived in the peninsula. In 1787, this post was
      assumed by the Sherif Galib ibn Musaid, who bore the brunt of
      the Wahhabi attacks into the Hijaz during the remainder of
      Selim’s rule.*^ For the moment, the Saudis preferred to avoid open
      conflict with the Ottoman forces, so they continued to concentrate
      their activities in the north and east of the peninsula, with their
      occasional raids into southern Iraq hardly noticed by the center
      of power as anything more than the usual bedouin attacks on
      settled areas. Sherif Galib was much more aware of the religious
      and political threat of the Wahhabi-Saudi movement, and he
      considered it his duty to do all he could to stamp it out before they
      became an important danger. His messages to Istanbul had little
      impact among the increasingly decadent and worldly members
      of the Ulema, however, and without their support he was unable
      to convince the Sultan that major reinforcements were required
      to quell the movement. At the same time he also was diverted by
      internal difficulties, with a revolt led by his brother Abdullah
      preventing him from doing much about the Wahhabis for some
      time after his. accession.*®

  In the meantime, as Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud and Muhammad ibn           225
al-Wahhab advanced in age, they jointly named the former’s son
Saud ibn Abd ul-Aziz as political and spiritual successor to pre¬
vent disputes over the right of succession and, just as important,
to assure a continuity of the loyalty of tribal and town vassals
should one or both of them die. With no effective internal op¬
position, the movement maintained its vitality and continued to
expand, and early in 1790, the elimination of the last important
rivals to their power within the Nejd, the Beni Halid princes of
al-Ahsa, set the stage for expansion to the north and south on a
scale not attempte/1 previously.
  Despite the absence of Ottoman reinforcements, as soon as
Sherif Abdullah’s revolt was put down, Sherif Galib organized
an army of about 10,000 men, including bedouin vassals sum¬
moned from all over the Hijaz and even a few places in the Nejd;
and in 1790 he marched toward Dariye, intending to eliminate
the Saudi threat once and for all. When he failed to take the
fortified town of Kasr Bassam, the lure of booty was effectively
dissipated, and the army broke up before reaching its objective.
During the next two years, Abd al-Aziz scattered the Nejd bedouin
tribes which had responded to Galib’s call, thus making very sure
that they would not respond again. At the same time the death of
Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, at the age of eighty-nine, left
Abd al-Aziz as undisputed spiritual as well as political leader of
the community. Between 1792 and 1794, he conquered al-Hasa
and made it an integral part of his state, and with its wealth, he
was able to build a regular administration and army for the first
time. The desert kingdom now was becoming a state, and the
danger which Galib had feared a reality. Wahhabi forces began to
move out of the Nejd on a large scale. Various groups pillaged
the frontiers of the Hijaz and of Iraq and moved into Katar and
Kuwait along the Persian Gulf, with their preachers going along,
arousing scorn for everything the Sultan stood for. The continued
Wahhabi successes and the huge amounts of booty secured in
these raids attracted the fealty of more and more tribes, including
many of the Iraq and Syrian frontier bedouins who were severely
harried by the raids and discouraged by the failure of Baghdad
and Damascus to defend them.^*^ As a result the Saudi army now
became by far the strongest military force in the Arab world.

226     Up to this time, the extent of the Saudi threat was not under¬
      stood in Istanbul, and the complaints, arriving from Mecca, Da¬

      Saudis still were considered to be no more than another one of

  As the century came to a close, all Ottoman efforts to check the
Saudis had failed. This dangerous political and religious move¬
ment ruled without check in most of Arabia. The Sultan’s failure
to punish it caused him tremendous loss of prestige in the Mus¬

                          The Balkans                           ^
  In the European parts of the Empire, conditions engendered by
two wars with Russia had led to the rise of numerous bandit ^
forces, often encouraged, supported, and emulated by the increas¬
ingly independent local notables. Between 1787 and 1795 in
particular, these "mountain rebels,” as they were called by the
Porte, expanded their activities almost without opposition in the
area between the Danube, the Balkan range, and the Adriatic,
and along the Maritsa River. Between Edirne, Sofia, and Bel¬
grade, the roads were infested by bandits who raided caravans,
travelers —and even military expeditions—and exacted heavy
tribute from the towns and villages which lay along their routes.^^
In Rumelia the most important chiefs of this sort were Veysioglu
Halil Usta of Dimotica, Dagdevirenoglu, and his ally Ali Molla,
who ruled the area of Edime, and Tokatjikli Suleyman Agha of
Giimiiljine, whose authority extended as far as Salonika and
Drama. To the north along the southern borders of Wallachia,
Yillik zade Suleyman Agha controlled Silistria and Deliorman;
Ibrail, Ismail, and the Danube shores between them were under
Nazir Ahmed Agha; while the areas of Nicopolis, Sistova, and
Ruschuk were controlled by Tirsiniklioglu Ismail Agha. The
lands between Vidin and Sofia were under Pasvanoglu Osman
Pasha of Vidin, whose forces also ravaged large sections of west¬
ern Wallachia and eastern Serbia. To the west, northern Albania
was ruled by Bushath Mahmud Pasha, notable of Scutari. In the

228   south, rule in Epirus was shared by Ibrahim Pasha of Avlonya
      in central Albania; and Tepedelenli Ali Pasha of Janina to the

                           Ali Pasha of Janina (I)

        Ali Pasha of Janina, descended from a Turkish dervish who
      had come from Kiitahya in the seventeenth century, was born in
      1750 in the town of Tepelen (Tepedelen) in Epirus, where he
      spent his early years. His grandfatjier and father were among
      the numerous district notables who ruled Albania at this time,
      but his father died in battle in 1763, while Ali was too young to
      defend his patrimony, so he fled into the hills and, like many
      around him, became a brigand, gradually building up his own
      band and raiding the surrounding area. At this time, the Ottoman
      governor of Epirus, Kurt Pasha of Berat, was attempting to sup¬
      press these bandits and, to get Ali’s obedience and cooperation,
      invited him to his capital and promised him the hand of his daugh¬
      ter. As soon as Ali disbanded his force and entered Ottoman
      service, however, Kurt Pasha reneged on his promise and a feud
      began which was to end only with his death. Ali then entered the
      service of Kurt’s rival, the mutasarrif (administrator) of Delvino,
      Kokka Pasha, whose daughter he soon married (1761). It was
      not long before the ambitious Ali attacked his father-in-law
      and then proceeded to take over his lands and properties, rapidly
      expanding his power in the area between Janina and the Adriatic
      coast. The Porte recognized his power in 1784 by appointing him
      governor of Delvino in place of his late father-in-law. At this
      point, however, Ali’s old enemy Kurt Pasha, still governor of
      Epirus, managed to have him transferred to the sanjak of Trikala
      in Thessaly, hoping to end his rise by removing him from the
      base of his power. But Ali managed to turn this move to his own
      advantage, acquiring considerable wealth and a large number of
      followers in his new dominion while still retaining his former
      possession. In the new Russian war which began in 1787, he
      rendered important assistance to the Porte along the Danube and
      in clearing Epirus and Thessaly of bandits, and at the same time
      he managed to incorporate most of the bandits into his own army
      while retaining the bulk of the booty instead of sending it to




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
Istanbul. On the pretext of pursuing bandits, he seized the entire     229
district of Janina and persuaded the Porte to appoint him its
governor with the rank of vezir in 1788.^^
  With this official position, Ali expanded his power rapidly.
                               ♦

Using the prestige of his military victories, he attracted, large
numbers of the local armatolis into his service, and managed to
use the wartime disorder to attack and kill his old rivals in Epirus
and take over their territories, one after the other. While the
Porte condemned him for these acts, it did not dare to act openly
against him because of his important contributions to the war,
so he was able to extend his power all the way from Elbasan in
central Albania south to the Gulf of Corinth.^® The only impor¬
tant resistance came from the inhabitants of the mountainous
regions along the coast of Epirus, in particular those of Shimari,
opposite Corfu, and Suli, in the hills above Parga, whose inhabit¬
ants had never recognized the Ottoman governors in the past and
certainly did not intend to accept Ali’s rule now. The Shimariotes,
generally Muslim, were ruled by their own beys, who fiercely
kept their independence of one another as well as from the Porte
and united only when they were threatened from the outside. The
Suliotes were mainly Christians who had fled to this region in
the seventeenth century from the lowlands of Epirus to escape
absorption by the Muslims around them. Protected by their lofty
mountains, they were divided into clans, whose chiefs exercised
executive and judicial power. All decisions of major importance,
particularly those of war and peace, were decided by an assembly
of all the inhabitants, who met together when conditions required
it. In times of war, these united forces were led by generals from
clans with traditional rights to military leadership. Since agri¬
culture was impossible in their barren and rocky land, raiding
their settled neighbors in the valleys was their sole occupation;
they also managed to collect a good deal of tribute in the form of
food and money from those who accepted their guarantee against
such action.
  The Venetian rulers of Corfu and Parga long had maintained
their influence on the mainland by encouraging anti-Ottoman
action by the Suliotes and Shimariotes who now, with the encour¬
agement of Russian agents, formed a loose confederation to resist




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1792-1798
230   Ali of Janina.^® Ali was not able to do anything about this until
      he returned from the Russian war early in 1791. Then he moved
      against the Suliotes hoping to catch them by surprise. But while
      he caught two clans, the rest escaped into their mountain fast¬
      nesses and soon routed his forces, inflicting heavy losses in men
      and prestige during 1792 and 1793.^® Having realized the difficul¬
      ties involved in conquering Suli, Ali abandoned his effort for the
      moment and turned to establishing his power elsewhere in the
      area, particularly to the north, where a new rival was rising.

                           Kara Mahmud Pasha

        In northern Albania, the principal ruling family was the
      Bushath. The base of the family’s power, was Scutari, which it
      apparently had occupied since before the Ottoman conquest,
      converting to Islam in order to keep its property and position.
      Over the centuries, there were many conflicts for power among
      members of the family, and it was only under Gazi Mehmed
      Pasha in the mid-eighteenth century (1748-1770) that family
      unity was established and its territories united under a single
      ruler.   He managed to gain power by acquiring large flefs and
      turning them into his private property, and also by allying with
      the Malisars (highlanders) against the Tosks of the south. During
      the war of 1768-1774, his son and successor, Kara Mahmud
      Pasha (1770-1796), was given the honorary Ottoman post of
      governor of Albania with the rank of vezir, and he performed im¬
      portant military services against the Austrians in the north and
      the Greek rebels in the Morea. At the same time, he and his sons
      built up the family power by entering into marriage and military
      alliances with the principal Gheg families of northern Albania
      while destroying those who resisted his power. By the end of the
      war, he had achieved such complete control in northern Albania
      that the Porte was forced to appoint him governor of Scutari in
      1779.31 His continued expansion and attacks on Ottoman gover¬
      nors and vassals alike, combined with a failure to pay his tribute
      to the Sultan, Anally led to an attack against him by a combined
      land and sea expedition under the command of Gazi Hasan Pasha
      in 1784-1785. Mahmud was forced to surrender, but in the end he
      was pardoned and restored as governor in return for large pay-

                          Ismail Agha of Ruschuk
        Ismail Agha was the brother of Tirsiniklioglu Omer Agha,
      notable of Ruschuk, who was executed in 1791 because of his
      misrule and his failure to pay tribute to the Sultan. The Porte
      replaced him with a local notable from another family. Ismail
      managed to escape despite orders that he too be executed. He
      then built a small bandit force of about thirty men, who ravaged
      and robbed in the areas of Ruschuk and Sistova for about three
      years. In 1795, the ayan of Ruschuk, then serving also as governor
      of Silistria, sent a large force against Ismail’s camp on an island
      near Sistova, but Ismail routed them, and with the resulting
      prestige he attracted large numbers of followers and emerged
      more powerful than ever.^^ At this point, through the intercession
      of the Hospodar of Wallachia, Alexander Ipsilanti, he was par¬
      doned and allowed to return to Ruschuk and live in his family
      house on condition that he give up his bandit activities and re¬
      frain from interference in local politics (1796). He honored the
      first promise but completely ignored the second. It took him less
      than a year to gather together his father’s old partisans. With
      their assistance he regained power in the city, and the Porte was
      forced to recognize him as notable. His power now expanded
      rapidly as large numbers of bandits joined his service, both those
      particularly attracted by the opportunities offered for booty and
      those defeated by the Ottoman armies and seeking some means to




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
recoup their fortunes. Within a year he also controlled Hezargrad     237
and Tirnovo and was the major power in central Bulgaria from
the Danube to the Balkan mountains.

                           PasVanoglu

  At the same time, Pasvanoglu Osman Pasha rose in the area
of Vidin as one of the most powerful notables of Selim’s reign.
The family originally came from Bosnia, but in 1739 Osman’s
grandfather Pasvan Agha vfas given two villages near Vidin in
return for services in the recently concluded war against Austria.
Osman’s father, Omer Agha Pasvanoglu, a member of the Janis¬
sary corps, inherited these villages and became a minor notable
in the area. Because of his rebellious tendencies, however, he was
executed by the local Ottoman governor, and Osman himself was
able to escape the same fate only by fleeing to Albania. Thus at
the age of twenty-five, he had lost his patrimony and was no more
than one among thousands of landless men then roaming the
Balkans as robbers and thieves in search of their fortunes.®^
  Osman participated in the war of 1787-1792 as a volunteer in
the Ottoman army and on his return to Vidin with a number of
his army friends formed a bandit force and began raids into
Serbia and Wallachia. When the Ottoman governor of Vidin tried
to suppress his band, Osman went into the mountains, built up a
large robber army, openly declared a revolt against the Sultan
and began to devastate the area. Within a year he captured Vidin
and built it into a major fortress. He now attracted into his serv¬
ice thousands of bandits from all over Bulgaria, Serbia, and
Wallachia, and also large numbers of Janissaries, driven from
Belgrade after 1792. He thus became the principal focus of all
the unemployed bands roaming the area at the time, assisting
independent brigands to attack settled areas, and reorganizing
and supplying them when they met defeat at the hands of the
Ottomans. At the same time, since most of his regular force came
from those driven out of Serbia by Selim’s reforming governor,
Osman became a leading opponent of the entire Nizam-i Jedict
program and attracted the allegiance and support of other op¬
ponents of the program, not only in the Balkans but also among
the politicians of Istanbul. With their assistance he was able to

      until he was ready to meet them in open conflict.®^

       Across the Danube, the Principalities had been left in devasta¬
      tion by the wartime campaigns, and the consequent famine and
      plague had been intensified by the exactions of the Greek Phana-

      During the decade following the peace of Jassy, six princes in
      Wallachia and five in Moldavia used their short terms to secure

      and family rivalries in Istanbul further complicating the situa¬

      coming across the Danube from Serbia, in particular those sent
      by Pasvanoglu and Ismail Agha. The peasants in the Principali¬
      ties were thus the most completely oppressed of all the Balkan
      peoples in this period.®®

      Bulgaria, Albania, and northern Greece, Selim was making a

  The Treaty of Sistova had left the Serbs in deadly fear. Long
years of mistreatment at the hands of the Ottoman Janissary
yamaks (auxiliaries), who garrisoned the country, and the Greek
millet leaders had led thousands of them to join the Hapsburg
army or at least provide it with sympathy and supplies as it
passed through their lands. Many Serbs had retired to Hungary
once peace was reached and the Porte reclaimed the lands south
of the Danube and ttie Save. Many more fled across the Danube in
the months following the peace in fear of Ottoman vengeance for
their wartime treason, and those who remained behind were
certain that they would not easily escape the wrath of the Porte.
  Selim III had no thought of exacting vengeance from his reluc¬
tant Serbian subjects. His main desire was to remedy the sources
of their discontent, in particular the power of the Janissary
yamaks, who in the past had provided the bulk of Serbia’s Otto¬
man garrison. He now felt he could use their inefliciency in guard¬

1793 he appointed Ebubekir Pasha as governor of Belgrade, with
the task of restoring its defenses, eliminating yamak strength
wherever possible, and above all, conciliating the local inhab¬
itants. His first order was to prohibit the yamaks who had fled
during the war from returning to Belgrade or anywhere else
in the province. He then not only confirmed the amnesty included
in the peace treaties but also invited those who had left Serbia
to return to their homes with guarantees that their former posses¬
sions and positions would be returned. While many of the Serbian
emigres accepted his assurances and returned, most of those who
had risen to become officers in Hapsburg service remained at
their posts at Carlowitz.

                      Internal Revolts and Foreign IFars
          XVI. The Eastern Question,
                         1792-1798




While the Ottoman Empire was not directly involved in Europe’s
wars for six years following the Treaty of Jassy, it was naturally
interested and vitally affected by the momentous events taking
place around it. The key issue of its foreign relations at this time
was its attitude toward the French Revolution and in particular
toward the new republican government, which was being ostra-           ^
cized by the monarchies of Europe. Since the Ottoman Empire,
despite its fragility, was one of the few major European powers to
remain neutral, revolutionary France sought its diplomatic ^
recognition as a means, however feeble, to break the bonds of
isolation forged around it, while its enemies strove with equal
vigor to prevent such recognition at all costs.
  The Ottoman attitude toward the Revolution itself was a curious
consequence of self-interest, utter ignorance of European condi-
tions, and pure romance. The Sultan was naturally disturbed by
the violent death of Louis XVI, whom he considered to be a per¬
sonal friend because of their abbreviated exchange of letters in
the years preceding his accession.' While the ideas of the French
Revolution were highly subversive to the entire Ottoman social
and political structure as well as to the position of the Sultan
himself, there was at no time any particular dread of them by the
Sultan and his officials or a desire to join the movement to stop ^
      the contagion. There were many reasons for this contradictory
      attitude. For one thing, in the past, the Ottomans had witnessed
      executions of their own sultans without the institution of the
      sultanate and the society which it maintained being brought into
      disrepute or question. Besides, even the most well-educated
      Ottomans were still sufficiently isolated from Europe that they
      could not only accept the events and ideas of the revolution as an
      "internal affair of Christendom, having no relevance to the
      Ottoman Empire, which as a Muslim State was immune to this
      sort of contagion,”^ but also as additional examples of the essen¬
      tial inferiority of Europe to the Ottoman system. In the end
      Selim’s attitude toward France was determined less by the new
      issues raised by the Revolution than it was by the traditional
      bonds which had brought them togethe,r in the past —mutual
    ^ fear of Austria and Russia and a common desire to strengthen the
      Ottoman Empire as the best means of countering the aggressive
      designs of its neighbors. At the same time, Selim actually went
      so far as to welcome the advent of the Revolution because of the
      very conflicts which it spawned, all serving to divert his enemies
      from his own empire while it lay weak and open to attack. But
      in the end, while sympathizing with France, Selim preferred to
      stand aside, avoiding alignment with either side and playing
      off the ambitions and interests of both to secure their assistance
      for his reforms.^
        To accomplish this goal, Selim required a more intimate knowl¬
      edge of European affairs than his predecessors had, so for the first
      time permanent Ottoman embassies were established in the
A     great capitals of Europe, first in London (1793), and soon after in
    \_Vienna, Berlin, and Paris.^ While these emissaries conducted
      some negotiations with the governments to which they were as¬
      signed, for the most part they acted more to gather information,
      while Ottoman foreign relations continued to be handled with
      the European ambassadors at the Porte by the Sultan, the Reis
       ul-Kuttab and the Bash Terjuman (chief translator) of the Im¬
      perial Council, a post invariably filled by a member of one of the
      Phanariote Greek families. So long as the Porte maintained its
      neutrality, Istanbul was one of the few places in Europe where
      representatives of all the warring powers were bought into un-

easy contact, and their struggles for the Sultan’s favor were, as
a result, especially vigorous and determined. The initiative was /C.
taken by revolutionary France. While its internal regime had
changed, its political position in Europe and commercial interests
in the Levant dictated that its basic policies toward the Porte
remain approximately the same as those of the old regime. Under
the direction of Talleyrand, these policies were pursued with a
brilliance and consistency unmatched by any of its rivals during
this period. While Ottoman recognition of the new government
was withheld in order to retain neutrality, France still strove to
restore the close ties which had gradually weakened after 1756 as
a result of the couft-inspired rapprochement with Vienna in the
last years of the ancien regime. By playing on the latent Ottoman
desire to regain territory lost to Austria and Russia and the fear ^
engendered by the partitions of Poland, France strove to per¬
suade Selim to re-establish the traditional French political and
commercial dominance in his empire.^
  To exert influence in the absence of a regular ambassador,
various means were employed. A French-language press was
established in Istanbul by French merchants, and regular reports
favorable to the new regime were published and distributed to the
leaders of government and other influential persons. Ottoman
requests for technicians and military assistance were generously
and promptly granted.® Stories were spread about Russian agita¬
tion of the subject peoples in the Balkans and continued Russian
ambitions to control the Black Sea and the Straits, and the pres-      (
tige of Great Britain was blackened by association. Bribes were
liberally distributed in Ottoman government circles to secure
policies favorable to France and to counter similar activities on
the part of her enemies. French emissaries were sent to Ali of
Janina and Pasvanoglu as well as to other notables in Albania,
Serbia, Bulgaria, and the Principalities to ascertain their situa-^
tion and secure friends wherever possible. And these efforts
gradually bore fruit. ^
  Even before recognizing the new French regime, the Sultan
and his ministers treated its unoflicial agents who had been sent
to Istanbul with an esteem and sympathy which excited the
envy and anger of the other powers. When the first French agent.

Descorches, arrived in June f793, the efforts of other European

  This sort of sympathy was as far as Selim went in the early
years of the decade. The experiences of the last war convinced him
that his empire could only suffer mortal damage from partici¬
pation in European wars, that no matter what guarantees were
given him by friends or allies, they would in the end consider
their own interests first and desert him at the first opportunity if
it was to their advantage to do so. While he appreciated that the

positive that it could and would defend him against the conse¬

formal recognition and dispatched an ambassador to Paris.
Although an unofficial agreement was made by which Selim

unconditional guarantee of Ottoman territory and assurances of

Erib Bey was still at sea on July 17 when the news reached Istan¬
