             The French Expedition to Egypt
  The course of French military action in Egypt has been the sub¬
ject of numerous detailed studies and need only be summarized
here. The original landings at Alexandria on July 1, 1798, wereX
not opposed.* Most of the Mamluks fled to Upper Eg)T)t without
offering resistance, and those who stayed to fight were routed by
the well-trained and disciplined French infantry at Rahmaniye
(July 13),^ and again at the Battle of Gize (July 21).** Cairo was
occupied without resistance (July 25), and Bonaparte was able to
consolidate his control of the Delta within a short time. But he
was largely unsuccessful in his efforts to catch and destroy the
Mamluks before they could move up the Nile and organize new
resistance in the south.^ As a result, while several expeditions
258       were sent as far as Aswan, Bonaparte never was able to gain firm
          control of Upper Egypt, nor could he even establish French con¬
          trol of its Red Sea port, Quseir.^ His effort to consolidate his flanks
          by conquering Syria culminated in a startling failure to take the
          fort of Acre, stoutly defended by Ahmed Jezzar Pasha with the
          aid of the Ottoman and British fleets and a large contingent of
          Nizam-i Jedid soldiers sent from Istanbul (March 23-May 21,
          1799).® Thus cut off from the east, Bonaparte was isolated from
          home by Lord Nelson’s destruction of his fleet at the Battle of
          Abukir (August 1, 1798).^ With the'expedition doomed to slow
          strangulation, Bonaparte and his chief aides abandoned it in
          search of greater glory in France (August 22,1799), while leaving
          its final liquidation to subordinates. His immediate successor.
          General Kleber, made an evacuation agreement with the Grand
          Vezir at al-Arish (January 24,1800), but this was overturned by
          the opposition of Great Britain and Russia, who did not want the
          Porte to make a separate peace, and who preferred to save Egypt
          for the Ottomans as the result of their own efforts.® Although the
          French subsequently routed the Grand Vezir’s army at the Battle
          of Heliopolis (March 20, 1800)® and managed to gain control of
          much of Upper Egypt by means of an agreement with the Mam-
          luk leader Murad Bey,‘® Kleber himself was removed from the
          scene by assassination (June 14, 1800). His successor Abdullah
          Jacques Menou attempted to establish a permanent French col¬
          ony in the country, but in the end a combined Ottoman-British
          expeditionary force obtained their surrender, and the final
          French evacuation was accomplished on August 31, 1801.“
      A     The French expedition remained in Egypt a little over three
          years. It was cut off from its source of supplies and doomed to a
          sterile existence within two months of its arrival. Efforts were
          made to liquidate it during its last two years. And yet, more than
          any other event or influence, it began the process by which the
      k long-established institutions of society and government in Otto¬
          man Egypt were overturned and replaced by new ones imported
          from the West.*^ This was achieved principally by eliminating the
          old ruling class, Mamluk and Ottoman alike, so that its departure
          left a political and social vacuum which had to be filled by new
          elements. How was this change accomplished? To what extent




                             Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
was it a product of deliberate policy, and how much was it simply       259
an inevitable and unintentional result of the French presence?
  French policy in Egypt was a curious combination of timid con¬
servatism and radical innovation and change, of professed respect
for native traditions yet a complete disregard for them in practice.
Bonaparte declared time and again that the laws, practices, tra¬
ditions, and customs of the Egyptians had to be respected by his
men, to whom he declared: "The people among whom we are going
are Muslims; their first article of faith is this: 'There is no God
but God and Mohammed is his prophet.’ Don’t contradict them,
treat them as you have treated the Jews and Italians. Have re¬
gard for their muftis and their imams as you have had for the
rabbis and the bishops. For the ceremonies that the Koran pre¬
scribes and for the mosques have the same tolerance that you
have had for convents and synagogues, for the religion of Moses
and of Jesus Christ . . . You will find here customs which are dif¬
ferent from those of Europe; you must become accustomed to
them. The people among whom we are going treat women differ¬
ently than do we; but in all countries, be wbo violates women is a
monster. Pillage enriches only a small number of men; it dis¬
honors us, it destroys our resources, it makes for us enemies of the
people who it is in our interest to have as friends.”'^ And to a
commendable extent these injunctions were obeyed.
  Basically and simply, the French expedition revolutionized
both government and society in Egypt by removing its ruling class
in a single blow, by substituting French and native officials for 7.,
the Ottomans and Mamluks who previously had combined to rule
the country. For however much Bonaparte professed to support
Ottoman suzerainty, the fact remained that in view of the Sul¬
tan’s declaration of war, the only way he could solidify his posi¬
tion was to fight Ottomans as well as Mamluks. French victory
meant the flight of the Ottoman governor and his men, as well as
that of the Mamluks, who comprised the majority of the adminis- 'i"-
trators and tax farmers in the country. In order to rule Egypt, the
French suddenly had to create an entirely new class of adminis¬
trators, tax collectors, policemen, and the like. The conquerors
alone could not provide all of these, not only because their num¬
bers were limited but also, and more important, because of the




                   The War of the Triple Alliance
260   need for persons who knew "Egypt and understood the long-
      established practices which they had to administer. So for the
      first time since the Ottomans conquered Egypt three centuries
      before, the Egyptians themselves were called on to participate
      directly in their own rule.
        Executive authority was divided between French military offi¬
      cers and councils composed of leading mercantile and religious
      figures in Cairo, the provinces, and for a time in the districts and
      villages as well. Each council was charged with legislating, main¬
      taining order, preventing quarrels among various elements of the
      populace and, most important, serving as an intermediary be¬
      tween the people and the French authorities. Thus in many ways,
      they fulfilled the duties performed by notables in Anatolia and
      the Balkans. But there was one essential difference. In Egypt
      these councils were only advisory, and the real military and p)olit-
      ical power remained in the hands of the French officers assigned
      to each place.
        The most important council was that of Cairo, which included
      among its members the Sheyh ul-Sadat, or leader of the seyyids of
      the country, and the head of the Azhar and leader of the orthodox
      Egyptian Ulema, Sheyh Abdullah al-Sharqawi. In addition to the
      provincial councils and the council of Cairo, Bonaparte also estab¬
      lished a General Council {Divan ul-Umumi) to meet periodically
      and debate issues of national concern. Thirteen provinces each
      sent delegations of nine men—three members of the Ulema, three
      merchants, one peasant, one village chief, and one bedouin
      chief—thus representing all elements of the population. The
      first General Council met from October 5 to 20, 1798, and dis¬
      cussed problems of organizing provincial and local councils, civil
      and criminal justice, the law of inheritance, and the tax system.
      It recommended various changes in the Ottoman tax system,
      including the abolition of all past illegal charges, but added that
      it felt the Muslim system of justice and laws of inheritance should
      be maintained. This council was dismissed because of its complic¬
      ity in a popular revolt against the French which broke out in
      Cairo and the Delta in the late summer of 1798. A second council
      was summoned in December of the same year, however, and fif¬
      teen of its members also were chosen to form a special council




                        Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
{Divan ul-Hususi), which met regularly thereafter to advise the          261
French authorities on the daily problems of administration.^^ As
a result of this activity, the people of Egypt, and in particular
their religious leaders, gained a desire to rule themselves.
  In administration and finance, the flight of the old ruling class
dictated the introduction of increasingly radical changes. At
first, under Bonaparte himself, the changes resulted less from
intentional alterations in structure and practice, as was the case
with the development of representative councils, than they did
from a complete alteration in personnel. Gone were almost all the
Ottoman treasury officials as well as the Mamluks who as tax
farmers had supervised cultivation and assessed and collected
most of the taxes before the arrival of the French. The Treasury
now was transformed along French lines into the Administration
Generate des Finances, and it was put under the direction of a
French economist, Jean Baptiste Poussielgue, who had been
financial director of the expedition since its landing. It was his
job to carry on the administration of the central Treasury and to
arrange for tax collection. The Muslim scribes who had fled were
replaced by Coptic money changers (Serrafs), who previously had
acted as financial experts, advising the Ottoman and Mamluk
officials but never holding official positions. The chief of the guild
of money changers, Serraf Bashi Girgis ul-Gohari, was made
intendant-general of the Treasury, with the task of actually di¬
recting the tax system under Poussielgue’s supervision. This dual
system at the top was paralleled all the way down to the provin¬
cial and village levels, as teams of Coptic intendants and French
agents went to each locality to supervise cultivation and tax col¬
lection under the direction of the French military officers and
with the advice of the local native councils.*®
  Bonaparte chose to retain the old Ottoman tax system intact at
first as the best means of securing as quickly as possible the food
and money needed to sustain his army. While reform might be
preferable, it would disturb the process of tax collection at a crit¬
ical time, so it had to be postponed, with French energies devoted
primarily to making the old system operate as well as possible.
But as it turned out the old system remained more in theory than
practice because of the departure of the Mamluks. Those few tax




                    The War of the Triple Alliance
          A

262       farmers who-were not Mamliiks and those few Mamluks who
          entered French service were left with their possessions, and they
          continued to carry out their traditional functions. But all the tax
          farms and other properties belonging to those Mamluks who re¬
          fused to cooperate with the French or fled to Upper Egypt, or both,
          were conflscated and placed under the administration of a sepa¬
          rate bureau of national domains. This meant that in fact most of
          the rural and urban sources of wealth in the country were admin¬

          created on French lines, the result was considerable alteration in
          the means by which taxes were assessed and collected in the areas

          were urged to take over the tax farms held by the national do¬

          direct system of administration by village officials thus replaced
          the indirect tax farm system previously in use, although for the
          moment at least the old forms remained intact.
      I        The old ruling class was gone. It was replaced by native Mus¬
          lims, in particular by the village chiefs and members of the Ulema
          and by the Coptic intendants. The Mamluks who had dominated
          the country for two centuries lost not only their positions but also
          their revenues so that even when they returned after the French
          left the country, they found the entire basis of their power under¬
          mined. Their revenues and positions were in the hands of native
          Egyptians who had been shown for the first time that it was to
          their benefit and interest to manage the affairs of their own coun¬
          try, a lesson which was not lost on them in the years which
              followed.

lem of how the Ottoman and Russian fleets should cooperate and

                  The Conclusion of Peace
  Even before the French evacuation of Alexandria, negotiations
to end the War of the Triple Alliance had begun. In Istanbul,
London, Paris, and Saint Petersburg, the politicians and diplo¬
mats were working to secure a definitive peace agreement, not
only for Egypt and the Porte but for all of Europe. In 1799, Britain
had prevented Bonaparte from transforming the convention of
al-Arish into a separate peace with the Porte, thus forcing Selim
to join his interests to those of his allies in the general European
peace negotiations then in progress. But during the late summer
of 1800, Czar Paul had become unhappy about his ally’s unilateral X
naval actions in the Mediterranean and rigid interpretation of
the laws of neutral shipping in the Atlantic and the Baltic. The
British landings in Egypt and the arrangement under which Ali
of Janina sent two regiments to serve under British command
there had stirred Russia’s resentment against the encroachment
of outsiders on what it considered to be its proper spheres of in¬
fluence, both in the Balkans and in Egypt. Paul therefore was
driven closer and closer to Catherine’s attitudes toward the Porte
and further from his British ally, and as a result in September
1800 he withdrew from the alliance."*®
  While the Sultan’s allies began to compete for his favor, the
Porte itself had been engaging in a form of direct negotiations
with the French through the person of its ambassador in Paris,
Morah Ali Efendi. Starting in February 1800, Talleyrand and
Ali engaged in a series of conversations on the question of a direct
peace between France and the Porte. Ali insisted on a prior French
evacuation of Egypt as a necessary prerequisite, but Bonaparte
said that this would be dangerous unless arrangements were
made to keep Egypt out of the hands of Britain and Russia. But in
fact, Ali did not have plenipotentiary powers to negotiate with

      his desire not to alienate the French, who, now that they were out
      of Egypt, could be used to counter British and Russian influence,
      and who also might attack the Ottoman Empire again, perhaps in
      the Balkans, if they were angered.®^ Bonaparte did all he could
      to widen the split within the Triplb Alliance by sending his old

      assignment of securing Ottoman ratiflcation of the Paris pre¬

      old position in the Ottoman Empire. He ’also continued to work
      through Russia, which was demanding that Selim accept it as a
      mediator in direct Ottoman-French negotiations to be carried on
      in Istanbul without British intervention.But Selim saw that if
      these proposals were accepted, he would alienate Britain and lose
      its support against possible Russian or French attacks.
        In Istanbul new political factions arose in response to the diplo¬
      matic situation. The Grand Admiral, now back from Egypt, led
      those who, alienated from Britain by the Mamluk problem,
      wanted ratification of the Paris agreement and conclusion of an
      alliance with France against Russia. On the other side, Yusuf
      Ziya Pasha, Mustafa Reshid Efendi, Ibrahim Nesim Efendi, and
      Ibrahim Kethiida led those who felt that the friendship of Britain
      had to be kept at all costs as a bulwark against both Russia and
      France.®^
        In the face of these diplomatic and political pressures, Selim
      sought to play the three powers off against one another as much
      as possible, using their conflicts to maintain his own freedom of
      action. As much as he might have preferred a French alliance, he
      saw that so long as the British remained in Egypt and the Rus¬
      sians in the Ionian Islands, they were a threat to his empire,
      especially since a peace agreement had not been signed. So he
      decided to ratify only those articles of the Paris agreement which
      would not offend the British, while asking the French to modify
      the others to bring them into accord with his allies’ desires. Ali

  The peace treaty between France and the Ottoman Empire was
finally signed on June 25, 1802, and ratifications were exchanged
on September 8 of the same year.®® Peace and friendship between
the two powers were restored. Provision was made for mutual
assistance in case of hostilities and for guarantees of each other’s
territories against all enemies. All prewar treaties and capitula¬
tion agreements were renewed, and French merchant ships were
given the right to navigate in the Straits and Black Sea in return
for the same right for Ottoman ships in French waters. Compen¬
 sation for war damages was to be determined by subsequent
 negotiations in Istanbul, and the existing customs duties were
 to remain in effect for French merchants until new ones could be
 agreed on. No mention at all was made of Egypt and the Ionian
 Islands since France had in fact been driven from both by force of
 arms.                                                          ^
   Thus the course of the diplomatic revolution caused by France s
 occupation of these Ottoman territories was reversed soon after
 their evacuation was accomplished. The Triple Alliance was

The Peace of Paris, like the peace signed at Jassy a decade be¬
fore, did nothing to help Selim put down the numerous provincial ^
revolts which were stimulated by the events of the war. They now
emerged to plague him with renewed vigor, thus once again di¬

                           Anatolia
  In Anatolia the situation remained relatively unchanged dur¬
ing and after the war. Chapanoglu Suleyman Bey and Karaos-
manoglu Ahmed strongly supported the Sultan and served to
quiet the brigands and introduce the Nizam-i Jedid reforms in
their areas. Battal Pasha acted as governor of Trebizond and
Erzurum after his restoration in 1798, and his son Tayyar Pasha
served the Sultan in the Balkans during the war, thus indicating
that the Janikli family also was now accepting Selim’s policies,
leaving Anatolia quiet.^
  With the death of his father in 1801, Tayyar Pasha returned to
Eastern Anatolia to take over the family possessions, becoming
governor of Janik and Samsun and Muhassil (district administra¬
tor) of Amasya, Merzifon, and Sinop. He also was appointed
284   temporary governor of ErzuruAi and Diyarbekir, in order that he
      would be supplied with the financial resources needed for the
      task of pursuing and capturing Gurgi Osman Pasha, former
      governor of Rumelia, who had now come to Anatolia and re¬
      volted. Tayyar accomplished this within a year; but instead of
      giving him the expected rewards, Selim took away a number of
      his lands and positions and limited him to the Black Sea coast,
      ostensibly at least because of the fear that he still might be in
      treasonable contact with Russian agents. In fact, this action was
      the result of intrigues of the Chapandglu family, which convinced
      Selim and his ministers that the Janikli family was becoming too
      powerful and would revolt unless curbed. The lands taken from
      Tayyar Pasha were given to Chapanoglu Suleyman Bey, who was
      thus made the principal Ottoman agent to curb Tayyar in eastern
      Anatolia, one more example of the old policy of "divide and con¬
      quer” as it was applied to the notables in the Ottoman Empire.
        But Tayyar refused to accept the Sultan’s order. He made him¬
      self entirely independent in his own provinces, ravaging the lands
      around to such an extent that he came to be known as the "chief
      of thieves” among Europeans resident in Istanbul. At the same
      time, he expanded his territory to Samsun and Amasya and de¬
      clared his complete opposition to the Nizam-i Jedid reforms, re¬
      fusing to allow the levy of men or provision of funds or supplies
      for the new army from the lands in his domain.^ By these acts,
      he gained the encouragement and support of Selim’s cousin
      Prince Mustafa, eldest son of Abd ul-Hamid I, who long had
      sought to secure the throne for himself through opposition to the
      reforms, as well as of Yusuf Agha and Ibrahim Nesim Efendi, two
      powerful leaders of the secret opposition among the ministers.
      They worked to arouse popular sentiment in favor of Ta5^ar
      Pasha and against those who sought to suppress him.^
        Selim now feared Tayyar might ally himself with Russia to
      assure his independence, so in the fall of 1804 he dismissed him
      from all his posts, and Chapanoglu Suleyman was ordered to
      lead an expedition against him. Chapanoglu’s army was organ¬
      ized and trained according to the new methods and armed with
      modem weapons, while that of Tayyar Pasha was more of a tradi¬

                          '   Syria
  While Mohammed Ali gradually eliminated his competitors

                                Arabia and Iraq

        The situation was far more threatening to Ottoman interests in
      Arabia and southern Iraq, where the Saudi-Wahhabi danger
      fiared anew during the last five years of Selim’s reign. Since 1799,
      a truce had been arranged and maintained between the Saudis
      and their principal opponents, Suleyman Pasha of Iraq and Sherif
      Galib of the Holy Cities, with the Wahhabis refraining from any¬
      thing more serious than normal bedouin skirmishes and raids in
      return for permission to participate regularly in the annual
      pilgrimages.
        By the end of 1801, however, Suleyman Pasha was a helpless
      invalid, and the strong administration which he had established
      was rapidly falling apart. His children were disputing among
      themselves over the succession, and his army had to spend most of
      its time fighting the bedouin tribes in the Middle Euphrates and
      the Kurds in the north.
        In 1802, Abd ul-Aziz and his son, Saud, took advantage of the
      situation to undertake a number of destructive raids into southern
      Iraq. Abd ul-Aziz then moved back into the Hijaz and captured
      and sacked Taif, which Sherif Galib left without defense when he
      saw the size of the attacking enemy army. For the moment, how¬
      ever, the attacks were limited to raids. Abd ul-Aziz retired back




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
into the Nejd with his spoils.^** But the attacks meant that war       295
had in fact been declared, and the Wahhabis were on the prowl
once again. Saud immediately inaugurated a series of raids in
Iraq and the Hijaz which shook the empire. In the spring of 1803,
he took Mecca without resistance after the heavily guarded pil¬
grims’ caravan returned to the north, and Galib retired to the
fort of Jidda without daring to resist the Wahhabi hordes openly.
Saudi rule was proclaimed in the Holy Cities. An amnesty was
declared and alms distributed to the indigent and holy men. All
the notables assembled at 'the great mosque, where the Wahhabi
precepts were read publicly and all present forced to declare their
adherence. The Saudi forces then spread out through the city,
killing those who refused to accept the new doctrines and des¬
troying tombs and other objects of veneration. All hookahs and
intoxicating beverages were confiscated and destroyed. Theolog¬
ical discussions were held between the Wahhabi preachers and
the local orthodox religious leaders, and those leaders who re¬
fused to accept the new doctrines were eliminated.
  Sand’s forces were unable to penetrate the strong fortifications
of Jidda and Yanbo, however, so they finally retired to the Nejd
with their booty at the end of May. Although garrisons were left
at Taif and Mecca, Galib was able to drive them out and retake
the cities within a short time.^” The Saudi gains of 1803 proved
only temporary. But the attacks for the first time made Istanbul
aware of the extent of the threat. Up to now no one at the Porte
really had known what the Wahhabi movement represented as a
political or religious challenge to the established order. The
Ottoman Ulema were so uneducated and ignorant that few of
them knew or cared about the theological debates inspired by the
Wahhabis in much of the Arab world under the Sultan’s dominion.
Militarily the brunt of the Wahhabi attacks had been borne by
nomadic tribes and relatively minor governors in Mecca and
Baghdad. But now they had ravaged holy places which the Sul¬
tan was supposed to defend as part of the basic duties of his of¬
fice. They had challenged the official state religion of the empire
in the streets of the holiest place of Islam. And when Selim finally
turned his attention to them, he found that they controlled all of
the Nejd, Bahrein, Lahsa, Oman, and Muscat, and were threaten-




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1799-1806
296   ing to take over southern Iraq, Hijaz, and even the Yemen. Their
      successes were attracting the allegiance of most of the nomadic
      tribes of the Arabian Peninsula as well as of southern Syria and
      Iraq. And these victories were inevitably strengthening those in
      Istanbul who long had opposed Selim.
        In the summer of 1803, the Porte took cognizance of the Saudi
      threat and tried to deal with it. Orders were sent to Hiisrev Pasha
      in Egypt and Ali Kethiida in Baghdad, ordering them to prepare
      expeditions against the Wahhabis as soon as possible; the gover¬
      nors in Anatolia and the Balkans wtere ordered to raise and send

      trines were sent to Cairo and Baghdad for distribution in the
      infected areas.
        But there was little response to the Sultan’s appeals. Jezzar
      Pasha’s death removed the one Arab leader who was strong
      enough to organize and lead an expedition of the magnitude
      needed to overcome the Wahhabis. The only immediate response
      came from Ali Kethiida of Baghdad, who in the fall of 1803 at¬

      Wahhabi suzerainty. But the rulers in Istanbul still did not real¬
      ize the extent of the Wahhabi military power, so Ali’s appeals for
      reinforcements were denied and he therefore had to avoid any
      sustained contact with the Wahhabi armies.And this was the
      best response the Sultan obtained. Internal political disputes in
      Egypt and Syria at the time prevented the local authorities from
      organizing any expeditionary forces. And the Sultan himself had
      too many other problems in the Balkans to allow him to divert
      significant strength from his garrisons there and in Anatolia.
      The way was therefore wide open for further Wahhabi advances.

      ravaged Medina and then moved into Iraq, routing the Shamiye

                          The Balkans
  Much of the reason for the Sultan’s failure to take decisive
action against the separatist movements in his Arab provinces
lay in his preoccupation with superficially similar, but actually
far more dangerous, threats in the Balkans during and after the
war with France.                 v
 Since Egypt and Syria were the main theaters of action during
the war, most of the remaining Ottoman garrisons in the Balkans
gradually were drained of their men and weapons to provide for
the expeditionary forces organized by the. Grand Vezir. To com¬
pensate for this loss, the Sultan’s only recourse was to pardon the
most important notables, such as Ali of Janina and Pasvanoglu
Osman, and appoint them as governors of their areas in the hope
of enlisting their services in suppressing the lesser bandits and
notables and of curbing their own ambitions. But with the ab¬
sence of Ottoman soldiers to enforce their obligations, the no¬
tables used these appointments primarily to advance their power
even more. As a result the other Balkan notables and bandits
were relieved of even the threat of official suppression of the kind
which had hindered their activities during the previous decade,
and they also took advantage of the situation to increase their
fortunes and territories. In the end it was only the conflicts among
those who sought to take advantage of the Sultan’s preoccupation
in the east which enabled him to maintain some sort of suze¬
rainty in the area until the arrival of peace allowed him to under¬
take more forceful efforts toward this end.

                     Ali Pasha of Janina (II)

  In the west, Ali Pasha of Janina took advantage of the War of
the Triple Alliance to build an empire of major proportions,
stretching from northern Albania to the Gulf of Corinth and
bounded by Ohrid in the east and the Adriatic in the west. In
1799, the Porte appointed him as governor of Rumelia both as
compensation for his failure to get the Ionian Islands and Al-




                 Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
banian port cities, and also to secure the services of his army        299
against Pasvanoglu and the other notables and bandits who were
infesting Rumelia at that time. Bitterly disappointed by the
settlement, Ali chose to ignore his new position, leaving its
capital, Monastir, in the hands of subordinates while he re¬
mained in Janina to concentrate his efforts on building his own
empire there with the help of his two sons, Muhtar Pasha and
Veliuddin. Although Ali was ordered to send to Istanbul all the
French officers and technicians captured during the course of
the campaign, he retained a good number of them in his own
service — building forts and batteries, training his infantry,
artillery, and navEil forces, and creating a lavish palace and court
for him in the European style.
  The establishment of the Septinsular Republic convinced Ali
that the Porte was determined to do all it could to prevent any
further expansion on his part. At the same time, as soon as the
Russian garrison established itself at Corfu, it began to follow
Venice’s old policy of supporting Ali’s immediate neighbors, the
Suliotes to the south, and Bushath Mustafa Pasha, who, since
the death of his father, Kara Mahmud of Scutari, had ruled
Delvino and Skopje while striving to regain the family posses¬
sions in northern Albania from his uncle, Ibrahim Pasha of
Berat. Surrounded by enemies, Ali entered into contacts with
French agents sent to Corfu and began to plot new means of
expanding his empire with French assistance. During the winter
of 1799-1800, Ali prepared to attack his enemies, with the Suli¬
otes at the top of the list. The French Colonel Charbonnel was
named to command his artillery corps. Albanian and Greek
peasants were drafted into his army and navy, which were
rapidly developed under French instruction. Ali also managed
to get the military support of most of the Muslim beys in Para-
mythia for a supreme effort to drive the Christians and their
friends out of Epirus and the Ionian Islands. While the news of
these preparations spread rapidly, Ali tried to conceal their real
object by spreading rumors that he was preparing to lead an
expedition against the French in Egypt.^®
  In the spring of 1800, Ali moved to the attack. He first marched
north against Mustafa Pasha in Delvino, and while he was unable




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1799-1806
300   to penetrate the walls of this'powerful fortress, the continual
      bombardment inflicted by his new artillery finally compelled
      Mustafa to surrender and promise military assistance. In the
      meantime the Suliotes, with Russian arms, ammunition, and
      encouragement, began to leave their mountain retreats for
      surprise raids into Ali’s territory, with devastating results.
      All’s agents prepared the way for a counterattack by taking
      advantage of dissension among the Suliotes, using bribes and
      rumors to get the support of a number, of chiefs, thus dividing
      their clans and making cooperation^difficult.^^
        In June, as soon as Delvino was safely in hand, Ali led an army
      of 10,000 men south against the Suliotes. Although they were
      taken by surprise, they were able to resolve their internal differ¬
      ences quickly and withdraw into their mountain retreats before
      Ali could cut them off. Thus began the last and most famous of
      the sieges of Suli. Through the summer and fall of 1800, into the
      winter and spring of 1801, Ali’s army surrounded Suli and tried
      to starve out its inhabitants. Charbonnel’s artillery tried to
      demoralize and scatter the defenders by a continuous bombard¬
      ment on a scale previously unknown to the area, but still the
      Suliotes held out. As the siege wore on, Ali himself began to
      suffer increasing difficulties. Shortages of food and the spread of
      diseases soon sapped the loyalty and ability of his own men and
      those of his allies. Many of the Greek conscripts in particular
      sympathized with the Suliotes and secretly sent them food and
      supplies, thus nullifying most of the effects of the siege. Nor was
      the disloyalty limited to the men. Charbonnel and his officers had
      agreed to remain in Ali’s service for only two years, and once their
      contracts expired they stole away and returned to Corfu. In addi¬
      tion, Ali’s main Muslim allies began to grow cautious as they
      realized that a victory over the Suliotes would increase his ability
      to suppress them. Consequently, they relented in their efforts,
      and as a result the Suliotes were able to secure fresh supplies
      from Parga. In the spring of 1801, the Suliotes persuaded Ibrahim
      Pasha of Berat, Mustafa Pasha of Delvino, and most of the
      Muslim beys of Shimari to abandon the alliance and join a new
      "League of the Chiefs of Epirus” against Ali.^*^
        In response Ali used the vast wealth which he had gathered




                       Internal Revolts and Foreign Wars
to undermine each of his opponents. He stirred a revolt among         301
the local beys in the district of Berat, forcing Ibrahim to return
home to deal with them. He gained the support of a dissident
group of soldiers in the Delvino army, who drove out Mustafa
Pasha, forcing him to spend much of the next year struggling to
regain his own command before resuming assistance to the
Suliotes. Most of the beys of Shimari were simply bought out by
All’s agents although many of them continued to provide secret
assistance to Suli. Only Islam Progno of Paramythia was entirely
impervious to All’s efforts and continued to support the Suliotes
regularly as the siege went on. With the league weakened, if not
destroyed, Ali tridd negotiations with the Suliotes, promising
them large sums of money and free passage if they would only
agree to leave their homes, but they invariably refused. He got
the Metropolitan of Arta to excommunicate them, but this did
not disconcert them in the least. All’s expansion was stopped in
its tracks, and, as his prestige consequently fell, many of those
whom he had conquered during the previous years attempted to
throw off his domination. Although the siege went on, Ali was
forced to dispatch many of his men to maintain his rule in the
north.
  To counter his loss of prestige, Ali turned once again to the
Porte, and in return for a pardon in late 1801, he agreed to accept
a new appointment as governor of Rumelia and to send military
contingents to assist the Porte against new difficulties which had
arisen to the east. But, feigning illness he returned to Janina
and instead sent his son Muhtar Pasha, recently named governor
of Lepanto. The siege of Suli went on, but attention turned to
Rumelia during the winter of 1801-1802.^**

                Macedonia, Thrace, and Bulgaria

been bottled up during the previous decade. Brigand armies, of
which the most important still was that led by Kara Feyzi,

                              Serbia
  Pasvanoglu’s allies also used wartime conditions to regain
control in Serbia. While he had promised Selim to end all raids
and support the Ottoman presence in Serbia as part of the ar¬
rangement by which he was pardoned in 1798, he was allowed to
leave his second lieutenant, Molla Idris Agha, as governor of the
Kraina, and this gave him the entering wedge he needed to re¬
sume his activities as soon as the Ottomans were no longer able
to enforce his obedience. Soon after Selim withdrew large num¬
bers of Ottoman soldiers to participate in the campaign against
the French, Pasvanoglu resumed his old ways, giving shelter to
refugee yamaks and sending them on regular pillaging expedi¬
tions into Serbia as far as Belgrade. The Serbian princes com¬
plained to the Sultan, threatening to flee to Austria unless order
and security were restored. The governor of Belgrade, Hajji
Mustafa Pasha, managed to quiet the situation during the sum¬
mer of 1799 by a campaign into the Kraina and also by besieging
and capturing a large number of yamaks at Shabatz, forcing the
rest to flee across the Save into Bosnia. Mustafa Pasha then told
the princes that the only way he could provide regular protection




               Disintegration of the Empire, 1799-1806

306   of this kind was to increase the size of his army and improve its
      armaments, which would require an increase in taxes; the choice
      lay between insecurity and high taxes. The princes objected and
      persuaded Mustafa to agree to an important compromise in its
      place. Instead of relying entirely on Ottoman troops supported
      by salaries, he would allow the princes to organize and arm native
      Serbian troops as auxiliaries, and these would be supported
      directly by the local population without the necessity of new
      Ottoman taxes. Thus for the first time'jn centuries, rayas were

          While the new Serbian units were being assembled and trained,

      Ottoman forces before the new local defense forces were ready.
      The yamaks moved from the Kraina and Vidin into Serbia and
      took Passarowitz, Semendria, and Belgrade against very limited
      resistance. Hajji Mustafa Pasha managed to hold out in the
      Belgrade citadel until the princes arrived with a large force of

      their Ottoman overlords, a unique action in the long annals of
      Ottoman rule.^^
          But this successful defense only stimulated new complaints

quickly from Vidin to the Morava, thus effectively cutting off

  The yamaks now established their government in Serbia on
the model of the government established by the military corps in
North Africa two centuries before. Rule was shared by Halil
Agha with four yamak chiefs, who took the title dahi* to indicate
their special position independent of the regular Ottoman hier¬
archy. To avoid punishment and condemnation from Istanbul,
they forced the Serbian princes and local Muslim and Christian
religious leaders to denounce Mustafa Pasha and his soldiers as
tyrants and declare their gratitude for the new regime.Under
Halil Agha’s direction and with Pasvanoglu’s support, the dahis
began a reign of tyranny and exploitation on a scale never before
seen in Serbia. They soon extended their activities beyond the
rayas to the Muslim feudal Spahis, who previously had remained
almost untouched by the political vicissitudes swirling around
them. Yamaks from Bosnia and bandits from Rumelia flooded
into the province, attracted by the booty they could secure in the
service of the dahis. The princes were deprived of all their official
powers and forced to watch helplessly as the new regime ex¬
tracted all it could from its subjects.^®
   With rebels in control of much of Serbia, Bulgaria, Albania, V
and Greece, drastic measures were needed. But it was only when
victory in Egypt was assured in the spring of 1801 that Selim ^
dared to defy the conservatives and do something to remedy the
situation.

Within a short time, however, Ali conquered the league army and
forced its leaders to accept his suzerainty once again.
  Since Ibrahim Pasha had failed to accomplish much in Rumelia
during the summer of 1804, Selim ordered Ali himself to go in the
following year, and he agreed because the Suliotes were out of the
way. While Ismail Agha was building up his power in eastern
Bulgaria and Thrace, and Pasvanoglu was occupied in Serbia,
Ali was able to chase the bandits into the Macedonian mountains
and re-establish order and security. But, just as in 1802, he took
into his own army not only many of the bandits whom he defeated
but also large quantities of booty, including most of the cannons
found in the forts which he passed. As a result, after his return to
Albania in the fall of 1805, Rumelia was even less able to defend
itself than it had been before, while All’s power and prestige
increased immensely.'^® To reward Ali for his services, and also
to satisfy his demands without forcing him to revolt, Selim
appointed Veliuddin Pasha governor of the Morea and Muhtar
Pasha governor of Thessaly at Trikala, thus completing the
family’s control of Greece as well as much of Albania. Only
Attica, Boeotia, and Negreponte remained out of his dominion in
Greece, while his court in Janina reached new heights of wealth
and grandeur, and western adventurers in his service trained an
army second to none in the area.®® Ibrahim Pasha now was the
Porte’s last hope, and in 1806 he was appointed governor of
Rumelia for the second time, mainly in the hope of providing him
with the power and prestige needed to counter All’s empire.
But the hope was not realized. Ali of Janina was supreme in
Albania and Greece.

                Disintegration of the Empire, 1799-1806
              XIX. The Eastern Question
                     1802-1807




    With the Serbian rebels moving rapidly toward victory, their
    fate, as well as that of the entire Ottoman Empire, now fell into
i\ the hands of the European powers who had interests in the area,
    and diplomacy became as important as victories on the battlefield.
      The Peace of Amiens had given Selim III a second respite from
y   involvement in the wars of Europe, but this did not mean that he
    or his people were removed from the conflicts of European diplo¬
    macy. The most salient characteristic of Ottoman diplomacy in
    this period was a gradual reversal of the alliances molded by
    Bonaparte’s invasion of Egypt and a return to the more tradi¬
    tional bonds forged by longer-standing considerations of national
    self-interest. With the resumption of the war between Britain
    and France in 1803 and the entry of Russia and Austria into the
    Third Coalition two years later, it was inevitable that this rever¬
    sal should begin and that the currently neutral Porte should be
    pressured for support by both sides.^


                          Foreign Relations

      Istanbul once again was one of the few places in Europe where
    representatives of the combatants could and did live in uneasy
    propinquity, so it became a center of diplomatic intrigue on a
scale not seen there again until World War 11. As usual Bonaparte       329
was most active. As soon as relations with the Porte were restored
in 1802, he appointed as his new ambassador his former comrade
in arms in the Netherlands, General Brune, with the mission of
regaining Ottoman confidence and restoring France’s political
and economic position in the Levant as well as obtaining compen¬
sation for the losses suffered by French subjects in the Empire
during the war. In addition Horace Sebastiani was sent on a spe¬
cial mission to Istanbul and the Levant with the object of formu¬
lating long-range policies not only to regain France’s former posi¬
tion in the area but also to expand it through the Black Sea, east
across Anatolia, and west into Danubian Europe. New French
consulates were established in various places to promote these
new political and economic ambitions. One of the earliest results
of Sebastiani’s mission was a French effort to expand its political
influence in the Arab world by championing the Sultan’s Catholic
subjects there, thus adapting the policy followed by the Russians
toward the Orthodox since 1774. Brune cultivated connections at
the Porte, not only to learn of its plans but also to influence deci¬
sions which might run counter to the interests of his master. In
particular, Selim was urged to maintain a firm policy against the
autonomous notables then troubling him because of the possibil¬
ity that conciliation would lead to the triumph of persons who
were under the influence of France’s enemies. At the same time,
however, agents also were sent to the same notables to make cer¬
tain that if they did succeed, they would turn to France for assist¬
ance against the Porte.^
  Russia, on the other hand, had gained enormously from the
Peace of Amiens, and the Czar’s main objective now was to pre-
serve those gains. The 1799 alliance with the Porte assured Rus-
sia access through the Straits to the Mediterranean. This, com¬
bined with its protectorate over the Ionian Islands, gave it
predominant naval power in the Eastern Mediterranean as well
as in the Black Sea. While it stayed out of the renewed war be¬
tween Britain and France, it tried to use its neutrality and alli¬
ance with the Porte to further advance its position at the expense
of both. But this was essentially a passive policy. Czar Alexander
I was anxious to make a much more active approach. Fearing the




                   The Eastern Question, 1802-1807
      A
                                    \              I               ,     .   ♦   »

330          effect of the rapid restoration of the French diplomatic position in
             Istanbul, he decided that the only way to counter this possibility
             was to resume Catherine’s efforts to fan the flames of revolt in
      '1     the Balkans in order to force the Sultan to rely more and more on
             his powerful ally to the north. Of course, Alexander could not
             encourage this sort of activity openly since it clearly would nul-
      ^      lify the efforts of his ambassador, Italinsky, in Istanbul. So his
             agents worked covertly and silently to carry out his wishes in this

               Great Britain’s view of the situafidn in the Eastern Mediterra¬
             nean, on the other hand, changed considerably as a result of the

             using the new situation to advance its position within the Otto¬
             man Empire. But Britain could not act openly to oppose Russia’s
             desires because of London’s need to secure the Czar’s support
             against France in Europe. Britain therefore worked to frustrate
           / Russian ambitions by urging the Sultan to strengthen his empire
             internally and thus enable it to resist subversion and attacks

               Sultan Selim was unhappy about having to continue to accept
             Russian protection and advice. The Czar had made peace with
             France in 1801 without consulting him in advance; he was aware
             that, despite its soft words, Russia was stirring up and helping
             revolts against him in Serbia and Greece. Russia had recently
             occupied Georgia and was beginning to threaten the Ottoman po¬

             less Selim still did not wish for a complete break with Saint

             want to rely entirely on Bonaparte any more than he wanted to

inform his negotiators that they could conclude a secret alliance

                               Serbia
  Much of the Czar’s reaction to the d’Oubril Treaty was deter¬
mined by activities in Serbia and Istanbul in the months since
Senyavin had arrived in the Adriatic. In Serbia the Ottoman
military preparations had caused Kara George to convoke on
December 1, 1805, "a second great assembly of all the principal
Serbian chiefs at the former palace of the Ottoman governor at
Semendria. Warning of the danger of a massive Ottoman attack
from all sides, he was able to get the assembly to agree to the
immediate formation of a national army, put under strict dis¬
cipline and trained by European officers as well as Serbs trained
in the Austrian and Russian armies. This new force was to be
maintained by a decentralized financial system, with each unit
paid and provisioned by a commune or district specifically as¬
signed to it. Indiscriminate demands for food by soldiers were
strictly forbidden under the penalty of death, and the siege of
Belgrade was pushed with new vigor in the hope that it might
be taken and fortified before the expected Ottoman offensive
could begin.^^
  The remainder of the winter of 1805-1806 was spent raising
 and training the new army and fortifying the strategic positions
 through which the Ottoman armies would have to pass to enter
 the province. In the east and south, this was relatively easy to
 accomplish since geography narrowed the possible invasion
 routes to a few places. To defend the Morava Valley against any
 attack from Macedonia or Bulgaria, a fort was established at
 Deligrad, thirty miles north of Nish, and in the rear Parachin
 and Krushevatz were siezed and garrisoned. In the Danube
 Valley, the choice fell on the island of Porech, one hundred miles
 east of Belgrade, which commanded all navigation at a point
 where the river rushes out of the Iron Gates on its way to the
 south. The western frontier was more difficult to prepare since




                    The Eastern Question, 1802-1807
there were no such natural dtefense points against attacks across
the Drina from Bosnia, but several small forts were established
along the Drina, and units were sent out from them to patrol
the river.
  Nor did Kara George neglect his diplomatic preparations. The
Serbian Senate quickly petitioned the Czar for arms and ammuni¬

the Russians in a difficult position. In Europe, their old friend
Austria had been humiliated, and the Peace of Pressburg had put
France in a position where it could threaten the Balkans once
again. The Serbs were intimating that they would turn to the
French if Russia did not intervene, so the Czar was in a position
where his entire influence among the southern Slavs would be
placed in jeopardy if assistance to the Serbs continued to be with¬
held for fear of the Ottoman reaction. In response the Czar was
considering a full-scale military occupation of southeastern
Europe. During 1805, an army had been prepared in Bessarabia
under the command of General Michelson. Selim’s recognition of
Bonaparte’s empire and the Austrian surrender of Dalmatia had
moved the Czar’s foreign minister, Czartoryski, to advise im¬
mediate preventative occupation of the Principalities, but Czar
Alexander decided against this for the moment until there was
more obvious evidence of Ottoman hostility to Russia. However,
starting in March 1806, under British pressure, a series of stiff
notes were sent to the Porte demanding an end to Ottoman mili¬
tary preparations and guarantees against any further favors to
France, with an implied threat of invasion if these measures were
not carried out at once.

then arrange to separate Serbia, Montenegro, Herzegovina,
Albania, and Macedonia from the Ottoman Empire and establish

ment of independent Slavic states in the Balkans as the first

abandoned, and Serbia once again was largely free of foreign
occupation. Autonomous Serbia thus had successfully defeated
all the Ottoman efforts made to force it into obedience once
again.

                     The Edirne Incident
  With the Serb rebels defeating the best armies which could
be sent against them, with the Montenegrins cooperating with
the Russians in their support, with powerful French armies
in occupation of Dalmatia and Ragusa, with Ali of Janina, Pas-
vanoglu, and Tirsinikli Ismail Agha extending their dominions
in Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Bulgaria, and Thrace, and with
the British, French, and Russians all combining professions of
friendship with threats of attack, Selim was in a quandary.
Danger lurked whichever way he chose to turn.
  To add to his difficulties, a dangerous new threat arose much
closer to home during the summer of 1806, making it impossible
for him to deal adequately with any of his problems. During the
previous year, Tirsiniklioglu Ismail Agha, ayan of Ruschuk, had
built up a major state in eastern Bulgaria and Thrace. This put
him in a position to threaten Istanbul and Edirne if he chose to
do so. Up to this time his ambitions had been limited entirely to




                  The Eastern Question, 1802-1807
346   personal aggrandizement, whfch he achieved under the guise of
      defending the Porte against Pasvanoglu and the other notables
      who refused to obey the Sultan. He^ had not been interested in
      internal Ottoman politics and had made no move to oppose or
      support Selim’s reforms. But with Selim’s order in 1805 for the
      organization of a Nizam-i Jedid army in Edirne through general
      conscription in the Balkans, this situation changed.^®
        At this point the Grand Vezir, Hafiz Ismail Pasha, moved
      secretly to use Ismail Agha for his owri^ ends. An agreement was
      made by which Ismail would capthre Edirne, march to Istanbul
      with his army and allies, and there help the Grand Vezir elimi¬
      nate his enemies and the Nizam-i Jedid. In return, Ismail Agha
      would be given large subsidies as well as an appointment as
      governor of Rumelia in the new order which would follow. Ismail
      Agha thus became a principal supporter of reaction and a threat
      to the capital. In early June he began to march toward Edirne
      with an army of 80,000 men, together with units sent by the
      notables of Macedonia and Thrace who supported him in his new
      effort.^’^
         In the meantime, the reform faction in the capital had arranged
      for the commander of the Nizam-i Jedid army. Kadi Abdurrah¬
      man Pasha, to come to Uskiidar. There he assembled 24,000 of
      his best men from all over Anatolia, ostensibly for service against
      the Serbian rebels but actually to provide the reformers with
      military strength in the capital in case their opponents attempted
      to use the Janissaries against them.^® On June 20, Selim ordered
      him to lead this army to Edirne, where he was to suppress the
      Bostanji corps, now ravaging the area in the guise of keeping
      order. He then was to leave half of his men to defend the city
      against Ismail Agha and go with the rest of his force to Skopje to
      assist the expedition against the Serbs. On his return, he would
      reorganize the whole Bostanji corps, limiting it to 1,000 men
      under strict discipline and with high salaries, so they would no
      longer have any desire or reason to steal. Instead of setting out
      at once, however, Abdurrahman remained in Istanbul for over a
      month putting on demonstrations of the new corps for the Sultan,
      and it was not until August 5 that he and his men finally set out
      for Edirne.'*^

            New War with Russia and Britain
  While the Ottoman government was in a state of flux, with

berats but said nothing to change his earlier declarations on the

                   XX. The Politics
                  of Ottoman Reform




It is not surprising that the many foreign and domestic wars
which Selim III had to face limited and frustrated his reforms.
But they alone would not have heen sufficient to defeat him en¬
tirely had not he and his supporters themselves created conditions
which made it possible for those with vested interests in the old
order to raise mass opposition to his efforts. In Selim’s time chronic
insecurity, disorder, famine, and inflation were normal accompa¬
niments of life in town and country alike. The misery in which the
vast majority of people were forced to live was in stark contrast
to the lavish western-style palaces and entertainments introduced
by the reformers along with European painters, singers, actors,
and writers imported in order to create an image of modern, west¬
ern life in their homes. Since these conditions were combined
with regular reports about the Wahhabi and Serbian revolts and
the triumphs of men such as Pasvanoglu, Ali of Janina, Tayyar
Pasha, and Jezzar Ahmed Pasha, it was inevitable that accusa¬
tions of "sinful innovation” and "infidel oppression” hurled by the
Janissaries, the Ulema and others, and their effort to attribute
these conditions to the reforms, should find ready response among
those whom the Sultan intended to help.*
  Much of Selim’s difficulty could have been avoided if he himself
had possessed a strong and dominating personality and had driven
                                s             I

        and led the reformers toward the common goal or, in the absence
368
        of this, if the reformers themselves had been characterized by sim¬
        ilar qualities of mind and body. But perhaps this was too much of
        a change to expect in a single generation. Selim III, although he
        had good intentions, was a relatively mild and weak person who
        sought to direct and control his subordinates not by strength of
        leadership but by the more traditional Ottoman method of turn¬
        ing them against one another in continuous struggles for his
        favor. In his later years in particular, iij response to frustrations
        and defeats, he gradually lost interest in the reforms and reform¬
        ers and retired to the pleasures of his palace, while leaving the
        reformers to fight among themselves as well as with those who
         sought to destroy what little had been accomplished.^
           The result was continuous political instability, which prevented
      \J the reformers not only from making any serious attempt to solve
         the wider political, economic, and social problems which accom¬
         panied and endangered their efforts but also from pushing their
         reform measures through to final success. During Selim s eighteen
         years on the throne, there were nine grand vezirs, ten sheyh ul-
       i islams, seven grand admirals, eighteen chief treasurers, sixteen
         reis ul-kuttabs, and nine bash terjumans, each with his own ideas
         and policies —and even more important, each with his own politi¬
         cal ambitions, which he sought to promote by means of the powers
         and revenues granted by his office. This was the greatest tragedy
         of Selim’s reign. The reformers split into numerous factions strug¬
         gling for power, which when obtained was used more for their own
         benefit than it was to achieve the policies which they originally
         had sought to undertake.
           The political factions and their alignments were constantly
         changing and adjusting. With the Sultan acting mainly to keep
         them equally balanced and to prevent any one of them from pre-
         vailing over the others for more than a short time, and with the
         factions themselves aiming mainly at the positions and revenues
         of government as means and manifestations of power, there were
         constant appointments and dismissals at all levels of the bureauc¬
         racy, the religious hierarchy, and the army. Efficiency, honesty,
         and steadfastness were the inevitable victims. It would be fruit¬
         less to trace the endless political maneuvers and alignments




                               The Triumph of Reaction
which arose during Selim’s reign, but the main lines of the strug¬   369
gles must be presented to provide some understanding of the im¬
mensity of the confusion which engulfed the reformers during
the period of his rule.
  It was only with the Peace,of Jassy that Selim was able to give
the reformers a free hand by dismissing Grand Vezir Koja Yusuf
Pasha (May 3, 1792) and replacing him with a puppet, the aged
and ailing Melek Mehmed Pasha, who was over eighty years of
age and entirely without power of his own. For all practical pur¬
poses, real authority was now in the hands of the reformers, some
holding official positions and some not, who met regularly in an
unofficial reform council as well as in the regular Imperial Coun¬
cil to debate, enact, and execute their reform decrees. Leading
this group were those who had risen with the Sultan and sub¬
mitted the reform memorials to him during the course of the war:
Chelebi Mustafa Reshid Efendi, lieutenant of the Grand Vezir
and originator of the Nizam-i Jedid army and treasury; Kuchiik
Hiiseyin Pasha, whose power rested not only on his close friend¬
ship with the Sultan and successes with the fleet, but also on his
marriage with Abd ul-Hamid I’s daughter, Esma Sultan; Yusuf
Agha, Director of the Mint, particularly powerful because of his
position as lieutenant of Selim’s mother, the Valide Sultan;
Tataijik Abdullah Efendi, who had a great deal of influence not
only as a result of the length and breadth of his reform proposals
but also because of his position as the only member of the Ulema
in the group, and thus Selim’s only hope of reconciling the re¬
forms with them; and three somewhat less influential men who
alternated as Reis ul-Kuttab to handle foreign relations, Ingiliz
Mahmud Raif Efendi, Mehmed Rashid Efendi, and Ebubekir
Ratib Efendi.^
  Almost as soon as the reformers came to power, began to enact
their decrees, and met some opposition, their coalition broke up.
Each man strove to divert popular displeasure onto his colleagues
in order to advance his own position at their expense. Less than
two months after the Peace of Jassy was signed, in April 1792, the
rivalry began when Yusuf Agha and the Valide Sultan got Selim
to take Kuchiik Hiiseyin out of the palace, appoint him as Grand
Admiral, and send him on a long naval expedition to the Mediter-




                  The Politics of Ottoman Reform
370   ranean in the hope of using his absence to end his influence.^
      Hiiseyin managed not only to counter this threat but to increase
      his power and prestige also by the spectacular manner in which
      he defeated the pirates then infesting the Aegean, and as soon as
      he returned in September, he got back at his enemies by using
      Janissary complaints about debased coins to have Yusuf Agha
      dismissed from the Mint although he still managed to retain con¬
      siderable power and influence through the person of the Valide
      Sultan.^
        Yusuf Agha then moved to appease the Janissaries and regain
      their support by securing the removal of Chelebi Mustafa Reshid
      as lieutenant of the Grand Vezir (October 1792). Although Chelebi
      Mustafa soon after was appointed director of the Nizam-i Jedid
      (March 1,1793), since he no longer was in the palace or the Porte,
      he was never able to regain the power and influence he had exer¬
      cised previously.® With Kiichiik Hiiseyin at sea and the others
      flghting among themselves, Reis ul-Kuttah Mehmed Rashid
      Efendi was able to dominate the councils of state until well into
      the summer of 1794. For the most part, he accomplished this by
      allying himself with the Sheyh ul-Islam Durri zade Arif Efendi
      and with Yusuf Agha against Kiichiik Hiiseyin and Tatarjik

      tion of the faction led by Yusuf Agha, so Selim soon moved to
      strengthen the other. In August 1794, he placed the blame for the
      current inflation and famine on Mehmed Rashid and arranged
      for suflicient public clamor to have him replaced as Reis by one of

      then allied himself with Chelebi Mustafa, went to Levend Chiftlik
      to help build up the new army, and soon after returned to the
      Porte as an official in the Treasury. But while he retained his
      place on the reform council, like his new ally, his power at the
      Porte and in the palace was lessened by his distance from them.®
      Then in October Selim shifted the balance further in favor of
      Kiichiik Hiiseyin by dismissing the powerless Melek Mehmed and
      replacing him with Izzet Mehmed Pasha, one of Hiiseyin’s own




                           The Triumph of Reaction
men, who was young, vigorous, wealthy, and politically influen¬      371
tial. With Hiiseyin dominating the council, Selim appointed
Ebubekir Ratib as Reis in May 1795. The Sultan soon moved to
limit the Grand Admiral’s power by encouraging the Grand
Vezir to rival him and build up his own power. Izzet Mehmed did
this by allying himself with Constantine Ipsilanti and Tatarjik
Abdullah Efendi, whom he brough back from exile and appointed
as Bash Terjuman and Kadiasker of Rumelia, respectively, dur¬

                           4

  At this point there were three factions among the reformers,
dominated by Kiichuk Hiiseyin, Yusuf Agha, and Izzet Mehmed.
With foreign relations becoming more and more important, the
ambassadors resident in Istanbul worked through these three
groups to secure the favor of the Porte, mainly by providing
their principal members with financial subsidies and gifts of
various kinds. As a result Kiichiik Hiiseyin and his chief allies,
Ingiliz Mahmud, Ebubekir Ratib Efendi, and the Sultan’s old
friend Ishak Bey, favored the French; Yusuf Agha, the Valide
Sultan, Chelebi Mustafa Reshid and Mehmed Rashid united in
support of the Russians and British; and Izzet Mehmed and his
associates, as well as many of the lesser members of the council,
remained neutral, receiving bribes from all the ambassadors and
shifting their support from one to another according to the polit¬
ical and military exigencies of the time.^® During the remaining
years of Selim’s reign, these alliances between the principal re¬
form factions and the foreign ambassadors remained virtually
unchanged, and they had an important effect on the Porte’s diplo¬
matic positions in these critical times.
  Since the factions were fairly evenly balanced in the palace and
Porte during 1796 and 1797, they sought to strengthen their posi¬
tions by outside means, and in particular by using the armed as¬
sistance of various groups in the streets of Istanbul. Kiichiik
Hiiseyin and his partisans depended mainly on the sailors of his
fleet; Chelebi Mustafa on the soldiers of the Nizam-i Jedid army
and reformed artillery corps; and Yusuf Agha and the Valide Sul¬
tan tended more and more to associate with the Janissaries and

      Jedid army. He also used the authority given him to build and

      Palace, who sought to end the war and restore the French alliance
      as much to lessen the power of their rivals as for any other rea¬

war, with the British-Russian party necessarily in control so long     373

  With the final evacuation of Egypt by the French expeditionary
force, Selim felt free to build up the French party in Istanbul once
again, as a necessary part of his plan to restore relations with
France in order to balance it off against the British and Russian
allies who had dominated him during the war. To accomplish this,
in May 1803, Ahmed Esad Efendi was appointed as Sheyh ul-

Kiichiik Huseyin Pasha’s party in the councils of state. Mehmed
Kadri Pasha, Kiichuk Hiiseyin’s chief lieutenant in the fleet and
commander of the Ottoman detachment which had cooperated
with the Russians in the Adriatic, was appointed in place of his
master when Kiichiik Hiiseyin died in December 1803. At the
same time, Ibrahim Nesim Efendi rose to take over the leadership

continued to be divided into three groups, now led by Yusuf Agha,
Chelebi Mustafa Reshid, and Ibrahim Nesim, who in foreign rela¬

respectively. For almost three years, following the war, Yusuf
Ziya managed to retain his position by using the prestige gained
by his defeat of the French in Egypt and by allying himself with
Yusuf Agha while at the same time retaining good relations with
Ibrahim Nesim and his group.

organizing a Nizam-i Jedid contingent at Edime during 1804 and

almost seven years as Grand Vezir. He was replaced by Kadri

originally one of Kiichiik Hiiseyin’s men but now a secret op¬

large party and prepared to take full power as soon as circum¬

376   empire. Selim’s role in successfully repulsing the British fleet

      remaining popularity rapidly evaporated, and Ataullah and his
      cohorts prepared for a final outburst against those considered
      responsible for all the difficulties in which the empire now found
      itself.
         But caution still was necessary. Selim and the reformers had
      preponderant military strength in and near the capital, with
      20,000 Nizam-i Jedid men at Levend Chiftlik, 5,000 artillery

      could get the support of the only other important military force
       then stationed near the capital, approximately 3,000 yamaks.

       were officially connected with the Janissary corps and, in the
       absence of the regular army, garrisoned the Bosporus forts. Their

under the command of the former Reis ul-Kuttah, Raif Mahmud             377
Pasha, now in charge of all the Bosporus forts, it seemed very

  Pehlivan Hiiseyin Agha’s mission became less important when

harbor and into the Sea of Marmara with the object of doing
battle with the Russian fleet and ending its long blockade of the
Dardanelles. With the sailors out of the way, the conservatives
had much more of a chance for victory, if only the yamaks could

  Rose Musa had carefully concealed his alliance with the con¬
servatives, and he now persuaded the unsuspecting Raif Mahmud
to try to win the yamaks over to the Nizam-i Jedid while the
Janissaries were still absent from the capital. Orders went out
incorporating them into the new army; officers were sent to train
and discipline them; and new western-style uniforms were pre¬
pared for them at the clothing factory in Uskiidar. But at the
same time, Kose Musa and Ataullah sent their own agents to the
yamaks reminding them of the glorious past of their Janissary
allies and arousing them against any sort of connection with the
"renegades, infidels, and bad Muslims” who composed the new
army.   So when the Nizam-i Jedid men arrived to train the
yamaks, fights broke out between them. As the bad feeling in¬
creased, the plotters saw that it would be not too difficult to set
off a.yamak revolt with only a single spark.^®




                   The Politics of Ottoman Reform
                  XXI. The Revolt




                                   V




The spark that was needed to set off a yamak revolt was unwit¬
tingly supplied by Raif Mahmud Pasha himself. On the morning
of Monday, May 25, 1807, in the company of a small Nizam-i
Jedid contingent led by one Halil Agha he went by boat to Rumeli
Kavak to pay the yamaks their regular quarterly wage and also
to persuade them to accept the new training and uniforms. But
as soon as Halil Agha began to distribute the uniforms, the
yamaks set upon him and tore him apart. The revolt had begun.
Mahmud and his men managed to escape by boat and land at
Biiyukdere, hoping to go on overland to Levend Chiftlik, but the
yamaks caught and executed them as soon as they landed. The
news soon spread to the yamaks in the other Bosporus forts, and
they rose to kill their officers and the Nizam-i Jedid officers sent
to train them. As evening approached, they gathered at Biiyuk-
dere, and chose as their leader one of themselves, Kabakji Mustafa
Agha, who immediately sent out the call to all the soldiers in the
capital to join the revolt and end the "infidel innovations” once
and for all.
  When news of the yamak actions reached the palace, Selim
called an urgent meeting of all his ministers and advisers the
same evening. While they were deliberating, a message arrived
from Kabakji Mustafa stating that the revolt would end if the
Sultan agreed to remove the Nizam-i Jedid men from the Bos¬           379
porus and order them to remain in their barracks. Selim im¬
mediately issued orders to this effect, thus again dismaying his
supporters and stimulating the conservatives to greater efforts.
Musa Pasha and Ataullah Efendi, still concealing their connec¬
tions with the rebels, did not want the revolt to end with this
concession, so as soon as Kabakji Mustafa’s message arrived,
they sent an appeal to the Janissaries remaining in the capital
advising them that the time had finally come to destroy the re¬
forms. The Janissaries then sent several of their elders and
officers to Biiyukdere, where they got the yamaks to agree to
continue the revolt until this end was reached, regardless of the
Sultan’s capitulation to their original demands.*
  On Tuesday morning,^ May 26, Musa Pasha met in council
with the other ministers and advisers. While they decided to take
firm action if the yamaks continued their revolt, he got them to
agree to keep the Nizam-i Jedid men in their barracks and do
nothing overt in order to avoid antagonizing the mass of the
people and perhaps causing the revolt to spread. Musa thus
gained time for the rebels to prepare their plans and secure
partisans in the capital while continuing to deprive the Sultan
of the only force he could rely on to resist them.
  Finally on Wednesday morning. May 27,^ approximately six
hundred yamaks set out from Biiyukdere and marched along the
Bosporus shore toward Istanbul, gathering vagrants and others
as they went. Since Musa Pasha continued to hold the Nizam-i
Jedid men in their barracks, there was no opposition, and the
yamaks marched along at a rapid pace. As night fell they reached
Ortakoy, where they were joined by three hundred of their
comrades who had come by boat, and they camped there for the
night. In Istanbul, Selim summoned Musa Pasha to the palace
along with a number of Janissary leaders and elders, including
one Bakirji Laz Hajji Mustafa Agha, himself a Laz like most of
the yamaks, who agreed to go to Ortakoy and use his influence to
quiet the rebels in return for a promise to end the Nizam-i Jedid
once and for all and to disperse its men. Selim thus sacrificed the
major accomplishment of his reign in order to save himself. He
now was certain that the revolt would be ended without further




                              The Revolt
380   difficulty. The ministers and a’dvisers left the palace and returned
      to their homes, and the Sultan withdrew to his harem for the
      night.
         Thus Musa Pasha alone was left in control of the government
      and the army, and he quickly used his position to good advantage.
      He immediately sent new orders to the Nizam-i Jedid men to stay
      in their barracks and to all the other corps to join the yamaks.
      Towards midnight Kabakji Mustafa and his men went by boat
      from Ortakoy to Tophane, where they^ were joined by the entire
      artillery corps in obedience to Miisa^s orders. With the Nizam-i
      Jedid immobilized, the sailors at sea, and the artillery corps
      with the rebels, the Sultan no longer was supported by the ma¬
      jority of the military forces which he had commanded only a short
      time before. During the rest of the night,and the following morn¬
      ing, yamaks came by boat to Istanbul, Uskiidar, and Galata,

      favorable to them, and spread a message for everyone to assemble

       palace. There they were to present their grievances but with the

       including Christians as well as Muslims, and that they would
       demand nothing that was not sanctioned by the Sheyh ul-Islam.
       Despite these assurances, it seemed obvious that the rebels were
      now on their way to success.
        On Thursday morning. May 28,^ Kabakji Mustafa, the yamaks,
      and the artillery men went by boat around the Galata point into

      of the modern Atatiirk Boulevard. The men immediately pro¬
      ceeded up the hill of the old city to Et Meydan southeast of the

      soldiers, artisans, and vagrants, coming in response to the pre¬

      no effort was made to impede their progress or to prevent the
      assembly. In the meantime the Janissary leaders met with
      officers of the other corps at the Siileymaniye mosque. After a
      spirited debate over the legality of their actions, they agreed to
      support the revolt and went to the Janissary barracks at Et




                             The Triumph of Reaction
Meydan, located between the Unkapani and At Meydan, where                381
Kabakji Mustafa and the other yamak leaders awaited them.
The city was now in panic. Those who did not join the assembly
at Et Meydan shut their shops and homes and hid themselves
and their families despite rebel assurances that no harm would
come to them. At Levend Chiftlik, the Nizam-i Jedid men took
up their arms and prepared for battle, but they still waited for
instructions to come to Istanbul and help the Sultan. But by now
it would have been too late even if such instructions did come,
for Levend Chiftlik was far from the scene of action.

While Ibrahim Nesim urged him again and again to summon the

that they instead be officially dissolved forthwith, and orders to
this effect were issued at once. Musa Pasha and Ataullah Efendi
left the palace and went to Et Meydan to announce this news just
as Kabakji Mustafa and the rebel leaders arrived on the scene
from the opposite direction. While the rebel leaders paused to
decide his fate, Selim ordered the palace gates entirely shut, and
he waited in his rooms for the results of the meeting.

the rebel leaders to increase their demands. After a short dis¬

declared to the assemblage that the Sultan’s order was not
enough; eleven reform leaders accused of various crimes, ranging
from killing Muslims in the Edirne Incident to violating Muslim
law and tradition in their reform efforts, would have to be handed

Reis ul-Kuttah’s Lieutenant, Safi Ahmed Bey; the Director of
Grains, Memish Efendi; and a teacher in the technical schools,
Lutfullah Efendi. Ataullah Efendi now revealed himself for the
first time; he issued a fetva supporting all the rebel demands and
sent it to the palace with the recommendation that Selim agree

382   at orice in order to save himself. There still was no public evi¬

      Ottoman society restored to the old ways, all would be well.
