      the only other survivors were the lesser figures who were with
      the Imperial army at the time.
        Finally on Friday, May 29,^ the revolt reached its culmination.
      Shortly after midnight the Sheyh ul-Islam and Musa Pasha
      secretly met with a representative of Prince Mustafa, and for the
      first time the idea of putting him on the throne in place of Selim
      was openly discussed and agreed on. Early the next morning
      Kabakji Mustafa arrived at the Janissary barracks with about
      thirty yamaks, and for the next hour he harangued the occupants.
      The Janissaries had been avenged for their long years of suffer¬
      ing; their enemies were dead, the Nizam-i Jedid destroyed. But
      Sultan Selim still remained: he who had scorned the traditional
      laws, persecuted the older corps, disdained the Ulema, and
      consorted with infidels. Now he had consented to their demands
      in the face of armed men, but what was to prevent him from
      resuming his old ways once the soldiers went back to their posts?




                           The Triumph of Reaction
The evil could be eradicated only at its source; to assure the
permanence of the reaction, Selim would have to be deposed.
The Janissaries agreed wholeheartedly, and they poured out of
their barracks toward the palace. Kabakji Mustafa and the
Janissary elders then went ,t0 Ataullah Efendi, who issued a
fetua authorizing the deposition on the grounds of misrule and
violation of tradition and religion.
  While the soldiers headed through the At Meydan toward
the palace, Ataullah Efendi went down to the Porte where all the
Ulema were waiting. When he read the fetva, they shouted their
approval and agreed to support the deposition. In midafternoon,
the soldiers and thh Ulema massed in front of the palace shouting
their support for "Sultan Mustafa Han.” At the same time,
Selim’s secretary Ahmed Bey was torn apart in front of the Porte
and his head sent in to the terrified Sultan, who then gave up all
thoughts of resistance and agreed to give up his throne in return
only for guarantees of his personal safety.
  Selim immediately summoned Prince Mustafa, who after
feigning reluctance, agreed to accept the throne. The Imperial
Throne was set up in front of the third gate of the palace, the
Bab us-Saadet, and the rebels fiooded into the great courtyard
before it. Late in the afternoon, while Selim retired to rooms set
aside for him in the harem, his cousin ascended the throne as
Mustafa IV, and the ceremonies of homage and testimonies of)"
loyalty were carried out. Thus the revolt had reached its goal, the
"infidel Sultan” was deposed, and his reforms could now be
dismantled.




                             The Revolt
      XXII. Epilogue: Mustafa IV and
           the Ottoman Reaction




                                       V




With Selim in the cage and Mustafa IV on the throne, power fell
into the hands of Kdse Musa Pasha and Ataullah Efendi, who
moved quickly to eliminate the last traces of the previous regime.
On June 3, the Nizam-i Jedid was abolished along with all the
new institutions and schools associated with it. Stating that the
reforms had been created by evil associates of the Sultan in order
to secure power and money for themselves, the decree declared
that they had destroyed order, violated laws and traditions, and
caused all the anarchy, misrule, and defeats which had torn the
empire apart during the preceding years. Hereafter, it was de¬
clared, the traditional laws of the empire would be carried out in
full; the older corps would remain to carry out their assigned
functions according to the established organizations and laws.
All the new taxes introduced during the previous reign were
abolished, and the older ones restored. The Ottoman Empire
would continue its friendship with its friends and bitter enmity
to all those who sought to hurt it.*
  At the same time, Musa and Ataullah acted quickly to stabilize
their personal power by dispersing those who brought them to
success and expected to share the fruits of victory. An agreement
was made between the Sultan and the Janissary elders and
leaders in the capital by which the soldiers returned to their
barracks and agreed to cease interference in state affairs in         385
return for assurances that they would be absolved of all responsi¬
bility for the revolt and that the reforms which they disliked so
much would be completely abolished.^ At the same time, to get
the yamaks out of the city, Kabakji Mustafa was appointed com¬
mander of the Bosporus forts on the Rumeli side, so he and his
men left the capital, leaving full power in the hands of the new
government.®
  While it was impossible to eliminate everyone who had served
the previous Sultan, almost all the important reformers still
alive were now denied office, and new persons were found for
most of the higher* positions in the treasury, the army, and the
palace. But it was not long before the victors fell out among them¬
selves. Musa and Ataullah soon began a struggle for power, with
each trying to get as many positions as possible for men loyal to
him or his party. Not all the Nizam-i Jedid men were kept out of
office; those against whom the rebel groups had no special griev¬
ance were brought back to the government, with Halet Efendi,
former ambassador to Paris, becoming treasurer, Chelebi Mus¬
tafa Reshid going to the dockyard as its director and chief of
the Naval Treasury, and Galib Efendi becoming Nishanji (chief
assistant of the Reis). Hurshid Pasha became governor of the
Morea and commander of the army based in Sofia; and Asim
Efendi was made official historian and chronicler of the new

          Preparations for a Spring Campaign
  With the armistice definitely broken, both sides did their best
to prepare for resuming their campaigns in the spring. In the
east a Russian arrdy moved into Anatolia, and on the Arpa Su it
defeated an Ottoman army of 30,000 men under the command
of the former Grand Vezir, Yusuf Ziya Pasha, now governor of
the province of Erzurum; preparations were then made to move
along the Black Sea coast in the spring.^® In the west, at the same
time, 10,000 Russian soldiers moved across the Dniester and
took up positions in Moldavia and Wallachia in preparation for a
new advance in the spring.^® In Serbia Kara George’s state now
controlled all of the ancient kingdom with the exception of Nish,
Leskovatz, and a few small places at the foot of the mountains
leading into Macedonia and Albania. A Russian agent, Rodo-
finikin, was occupied with reorganizing the government and
army, and special efforts were being made to organize the popula¬
tion en masse and to transform the various semi-independent
rebel bands into regular disciplined regiments under a central
command.^’^
  Nor did the Ottomans neglect their preparations. Orders were
sent out to Anatolia, Bosnia, and Macedonia for troops to be raised
and sent for the spring campaign. Hundreds of men were soon
crossing the Bosporus and moving through the capital on their
way to Edirne. In Bosnia the governor had a force of 10,000 men
ready at Travnik to move toward the Drina. Efforts were made
to replace Yusuf Pasha at Erzurum and send him as governor to
Baghdad, but when he refused to leave, he was retained in his
post and ordered to regroup his army as soon as possible.^® On
March 23, a full Imperial Council, meeting at the Porte in the

  While conditions were ostensibly returning to normal in Istan¬
 bul, and the Imperial army along the Danube prepared for the
  spring campaign, momentous efforts were being made at Ruschuk
 to reverse the reaction and restore Selim to the throne from which
  he had been so abruptly removed the year before.
    While most of the Nizam-i Jedid leaders had been either killed
  or absorbed by the reaction, their subordinates had been with the
  Imperial army at the time of the revolt. Most of them moved
 back to Ruschuk with Bayrakdar Mustafa Pasha when he split
 with the Grand Vezir and returned home in early July 1807.
y There they accepted his protection, and with his approval and
  inspiration, they formed a secret committee with the aim of re-
^ storing Selim and reviving his reforms.* Led by Bayrakdar
 Mustafa himself, the committee included Mustafa Refik Efendi,^
 a member of the scribal class who had served as Lieutenant of the
  Grand Vezir immediately before the revolution, Mehmed Said
 Galib Efendi,^ Chief Assistant of the current Grand Vezir and
 ostensibly stationed at Ruschuk to carry on the negotiations
 with the Russians at Slobosia; Abdullah Ramiz Efendi,^ a mem¬
 ber of the Ulema who had served as judge of the expeditionary
 force sent against the French in Egypt before entering the scribal
 class and serving as supervisor of the Mortar corps and Chief
Accountant in the Treasury before the revolution; Mehmed             397
Tahsin Efendi,® also originally a member of the Ulema, who had
transferred to the scribal class and risen to be secretary of the
Grand Vezir at the time of the revolution; and Mehmed Emin
Behij Efendi,® who as chief buyer of the Imperial army in 1806
and 1807 had come into close contact with Bayrakdar Mustafa
during the course of the campaigns. The moving intellectual force
behind the committee was Ramiz Efendi, who wrote a long report
to Bayrakdar describing the foreign and domestic situation at
that time, praising the virtues of Selim and his reforms and
urging his restoration in order to save the empire.
  Ba3u-akdar Mustafa was hardly an intellectual, nor was he a
strong partisan of reform. His beloved master, Ismail Agha, had
ended his life as a firm opponent of everything Selim stood for,
and most of his fellow notables, led by Pasvanoglu, had con¬
stantly opposed the reforms as direct threats to their autonomy
and power. In a sense, his new emphasis was not as much a de¬
parture from their policies as might be imagined. The notables
had maintained and emphasized their autonomy by opposing
those in power in Istanbul, and they had secured their following
mainly from among Janissaries and others who had suffered at
the hands of government, so they opposed reform. But now it was
the Janissaries and reactionaries who ruled in Istanbul, and once
in power they disliked ayan autonomy in the Balkans just as
much as Selim had. It was therefore natural for Alemdar Mustafa
and his friends to support Istanbul’s opponents, who now were
represented by Selim’s partisans. He was won over by their
preaching and gave full support to their plans.
  The committee members decided almost at the start that the
only way to accomplish their ends would be to bring Bayrakdar’s
army to Istanbul to overcome their enemies by force. But this
was not possible without sacrificing the life of their hero Selim,
who was completely in the hands of his cousin. The Sultan would
hardly welcome the unexpected arrival of an army from Ruschuk.
He would most certainly execute Selim and his cousin Mahmud
in order to leave himself as the only male member of the Ottoman
dynasty and thus to assure his position regardless of who was in
power. In order to solve this problem, the committee decided to

  While the Sultan encouraged the Ruschuk committee, he also
worked in other directions to preserve his own position. Within
a short time he won the support of Tayyar Pasha with the promise
of the Grand Vezirate if he was able to get rid of the domination of
his patron, Ataullah Efendi. Preparations were made to replace
Ataullah with Osman Pasha zade Izzet Bey, Kadiasker of Anatolia,
but so long as the Janissaries supported Ataullah, this was post¬
poned as impractical. The Sultan also worked through Chelebi
Mustafa Pasha, plotting with him and Tayyar to secure the
assassination of both princes in the palace so that he would re¬
main as the sole surviving male Ottoman. But Ataullah found
out about the Sultan’s dealings with Tayyar Pasha and used the
threat of a new Janissary uprising and a revolt against Tayyar in
eastern Anatolia by Chapanoglu Suleyman and Yusuf Ziya to
secure his dismissal on March 21, 1808.Ataullah was stronger




                    The Deposition of Mustafa TV
400   than ever; he had got rid of Musa Pasha and of Musa’s replace¬
      ment, Tayyar Pasha. Yusuf Ziya and Suleyman Pasha were
      overjoyed. But Tayyar was bitter a'gainst Chelebi Mustafa and
      Ataullah Efendi, and when he reached his place of exile, he soon
      got into communication with Bayrakdar Mustafa, who promised
      to protect him in return for his help and got Istanbul to appoint
      him military governor of Varna at the end of April.At this
      point Mustafa IV worked to strengthen the Ruschuk committee
      and get its support against Ataullah by promoting Refik Efendi
      to be Lieutenant of the Grand Vhzir in Istanbul and replacing
      him as Reis ul-Kuttab by Galib Efendi. Tahsin Efendi also was
      brought to Istanbul as Chief of the Chavush Corps, and Behij
      Efendi remained Chief Accountant. By this time four members of
      the committee were with the Grand Vezir, and only Ramiz Efendi
      remained in Ruschuk with Bayrakdar Mustafa.
        Refik Efendi now discovered that Yilik Suleyman, Gavur
      Hasan, and Ahmed Agha were still at Edirne. He informed
      Bayrakdar Mustafa, who immediately marched there with a
      force of 10,000 men on the pretext of going on a hunt. This sud¬
      den move frightened the Sultan and Grand Vezir as much as it
      surprised the Ruschuk committee members. Mustafa IV decided
      to temporize rather than force trouble, so he ordered Chelebi Mus¬
      tafa to get rid of Bayrakdar Mustafa’s enemies, who immediately
      left Edirne and returned to their homes.Mustafa was still not
      satisfied. He decided to use the occasion to get rid of the Grand
      Vezir as well and sent a series of complaints against him to Istan¬
      bul, and Chelebi Mustafa also sent complaints about the notable
      of Ruschuk. The committee now worked to bridge the dispute
      since it needed the help and cooperation of both men. Behij Efendi
      finally managed to smooth over the situation and arrange an
      agreement. Bayrakdar Mustafa would retain command of the
      Danube army, and the Grand Vezir would stay with the Imperial
      army in Edirne; when necessary he would send assistance to
      both the Serbian and Russian fronts although he himself would
      come only if requested to do so by Mustafa.*®
        Behij Efendi then went on to Istanbul, where he worked to get
      not only the Sultan’s approval for this agreement but also his
      permission for Bayrakdar to come with his army to carry out the




                           The Triumph of Reaction
plans they had discussed earlier. The committee for some time           401
had developed good relations with two of the Sultan’s closest
associates, Guiju Fettah Efendi and Nezar Agha, both officials in
the palace, who now supported Behij’s claim that Bayrakdar was
loyal to the Sultan and would .only act to support him against the
tyrants before returning to the Danube. The Sultan demanded
however that Selim and possibly Prince Mahmud also be assassi¬
nated before Bayrakdar Mustafa came to the city. Behij Efendi
resisted this idea, but to retain his credit with the Sultan, he
                             4

based his opposition on the assumption that so long as the people
of Istanbul, the notables of Anatolia and the Balkans, and the
mass of soldiers \^ere opposed, assassination was not possible
without stirring up a new revolt which might end the dynasty
altogether. He finally convinced the Sultan, but still Bayrakdar’s
permission to march was withheld.'^ Behij Efendi was appointed
Treasurer (May 7) so he could use the Imperial Treasury and its
salaries to stifle any effort by the military corps to oppose Bayrak¬
dar. Bayrakdar now came to Edirne on the pretext of discussing
spring campaign plans with the Grand Vezir but actually to
arrange the march on Istanbul while at the same time taking
care that the Russian army did not take advantage of the situa¬
tion to move across the Danube.*®
  Ataullah Efendi and his creatures in Istanbul, frightened by
the presence of such a large force in Edirne, ordered both Chelebi
and Bayrakdar Mustafa to go to the front at once in anticipation
of a Russian attack. The two commanders decided to leave the
bulk of the regular army at Edirne while they themselves
marched to Istanbul with approximately 15,000 men from the
Ruschuk army on the pretext of going to discuss with the Sultan a
shortage of supplies and the consequent increasing disorder in
the Balkan armies and garrisons.*®
  On Thursday, July 14, the army set out for the capital, with the
Grand Vezir leading the way and Bayrakdar Mustafa and the
members of the Ruschuk committee following. In order that
Ataullah not be forewarned of the march any earlier than neces¬
sary, arrangements were made to suspend all communications
and close all the roads between Edirne and the capital. As the
army marched along, only its commanders knew where it was




                    The Deposition of Mustafa IV
402   going. Secret messages were sent to Fettah and Nezar for de¬
      livery to the Sultan, stating that the army had fallen into dis¬
      order as a result of supply problems dnd that the two commanders
      were merely coming to Istanbul to discuss the matter with the
      Sultan. Bayrakdar also sent Hajji Ali Agha, notable of Pin-
      arhisar, with a group of horsemen who set out overland to Rumeli
      Feneri, where they attacked and killed Kabakji Mustafa, cut
      off his head, and scattered his men. This action effectively pre¬
      vented the yamaks from moving intp Istanbul to save their allies
      when the crisis came.^”           '
        On July 18, the advancing army reached Silivri, and it seemed
      certain to arrive at the capital the next morning. Mustafa IV
      met with the Sheyh ul-Islam and Kaymakam in the palace and
      called a formal council meeting for the next morning to discuss
      the march, which had been carried out without his permission.
      But the next morning the council decided that since the Grand
      Vezir and Bayrakdar Mustafa had come this far, nothing could
      be done, so they proceeded directly through the city and outside
      the walls to meet them.^‘
        On the afternoon of Tuesday, July 19, the Grand Vezir and
      Bayrakdar Mustafa were first received by Ataullah Efendi and
      the other state leaders, after which the Sultan formally received
      them. Since Ataullah had failed to stop Bayrakdar, he now tried
      to secure his support, and proposed an alliance against the Grand
      Vezir, who would then be replaced by Bayrakdar both as Grand
      Vezir and commander of the Imperial army. Bayrakdar rejected
      the offer out of hand.^^ The Sultan then returned to his palace
      followed by the Grand Vezir and the state officials. Bayrakdar
      Mustafa and his army set up camp outside the city walls at
      Chirpiji, where they remained for two nights while the members
      of the Ruschuk committee entered the city to prepare for their
      arrival. Finally, on July 21, Bayrakdar entered Istanbul with a
      force of between 3,000 and 5,000 men. He immediately met the
      Grand Vezir, who got the Sultan to dismiss Ataullah and replace
      him with Arab zade Arif Efendi. With Bayrakdar’s men stationed
      at key places throughout the city, the Janissaries were kept
      effectively under check, and there was no effort to oppose the
      order. By secret agreement Bayrakdar and the Grand Vezir




                           The Triumph of Reaction
planned to punish the tyrants who had opposed the Sultan and          403
mixed in state affairs, and then Bayrakdar and his men would
return to their regular duties on the Danube. In the days which
followed, they set to their work with a vengeance. Most of the
Ulema and others who had played important roles in Selim’s
deposition were exiled, and the Janissaries and yamaks who had
participated in the riots were put down; within a week all opposi¬
tion was ended. The Grand Vezir was very happy because he
finally had sufficient power, to administer the government with¬
out any opposition at all.^^
  But it was not long before Bayrakdar Mustafa and the Grand
Vezir split on the question of whether or not the Ruschuk army
should return home now that its work was done. The immediate
spark for the quarrel came over the question of the Grand Admi¬
ral, Seydi Ali Pasha, who the Ruschuk committee said had been
in close relations with Ataullah Efendi and should be dismissed.
The Grand Vezir considered Seydi Ali one of his chief supporters
and refused to dismiss him, insisting on his right to make final
decisions on such matters. Bayrakdar was enraged and said
that none of the tyrants could be pardoned if the evil was to be
eradicated and the state saved from those who would usurp
power.Bayrakdar Mustafa and the Ruschuk committee mem¬
bers now worked to get Selim out of the palace so they could
put him on the throne and depose both the Sultan and the Grand
Vezir. Early on the morning of July 27, however, Chelebi Mustafa
learned of this plan from spies in Bayrakdar’s army. At long
last he realized what was happening and what had been planned
all along, and he sent a message to this effect to the Sultan. But
Mustafa IV did not take the message seriously, and did nothing
about it. Chelebi Mustafa then moved to act on his own, if not
against Selim at least against the Ruschuk committee members.
He got Nezar Agha to agree that all committee members in the
city should be killed during the night and the gates closed against
Bayrakdar Mustafa and Ramiz Efendi, who were camping with
their men outside the walls. Since Nezar Agha still believed in
Bayrakdar and thought he had come to Istanbul to kill Selim,
not save him, he stated that the Grand Vezir was mistaken and
left the Porte without taking any action. He then immediately




                   The Deposition of Mustafa IV
404   informed the Ruschuk committee and Bayrakdar of his talks
      with the Grand Vezir, and they decided to take direct action as
                                           V

      soon as possible.^®
        On the morning of July 28, Bayrakdar Mustafa and Ramiz
      Efendi marched into Istanbul with the entire army of 15,000 men.
      When it arrived at the Bayezid mosque, the force was divided,
      with one group moving across the peak of the Istanbul hill di¬
      rectly toward Et Meydan and the palape, and the other descend¬
      ing the slopes to the Porte to take control of it before moving to
      join their commander at the palace. By noon the Grand Vezir had
      heard the news and closed the gates of the Porte. When he refused
      to open them, Bayrakdar’s men broke them down, forced him to
      turn over the seal of office, and then sent him out of the city.^®
      On the advice of Ramiz Efendi, Bayrakd’ar summoned the Sheyh
      ul-Islam and other leaders of the Ulema to the Porte and got
      them to agree to restore Selim and to accompany him up the hill
      to the palace. Early in the afternoon, this group went into the
      palace and marched up to the Bab as-Saadet gate. Bayrakdar
      Mustafa and his entourage withdrew into the imperial council’s
      meeting room and told the Sheyh ul-Islam to go to Mustafa, and
      persuade him to abdicate his position and to send Selim out to
      them so he could be restored to the throne. Here Bayrakdar
      Mustafa made his fatal mistake. Mustafa IV refused to listen to
      the Sheyh ul-Islam, accused him of conspiring with the rebels,
      and sent him back to Bayrakdar Mustafa in terror. Before
      Bayrakdar could muster his forces and move to enforce his revolt,
      Mustafa had the gates closed, and he immediately sent his per¬
      sonal slaves to assassinate both Selim and Mahmud. Selim was
      caught in his apartment and killed after a short struggle; but
      Prince Mahmud was forewarned sufficiently to escape the assas¬
      sins and flee over the roofs to Bayrakdar Mustafa, who immedi¬
      ately placed him on the throne as soon as he learned of Selim’s
      fate.^^
        Selim’s death was apparently the result of two fatal blunders on
      the part of the plotters; they had failed to act for a week, giving
      the Sultan and Ataullah a chance to find out what was happening
      and arrange resistance, and when they moved into the palace,
      instead of attacking at once, they tried to mediate a settlement,




                           The Triumph of Reaction
thus giving Mustafa a chance to get rid of Selim. Mustafa now         405
was dethroned after a reign of little over a year, and in his place
Prince Mahmud ascended the throne as Mahmud II. The rebels
were successful, but now they had to work to restore the Nizam-i
Jedid through the offices of an unknown and untried young
prince. With Mahmud’s accession a new and eventually much
more successful and fruitful period of Ottoman history was
begun, and Selim’s era came to an end.


  Despite indications that Selim was a "modernist” in many
ways, the evidence at hand seems to indicate strongly that he
was a man of his time and no more, that at most he was a link
between the traditionalist reformers who preceded and the mod¬
ernist reformers who followed.
  Selim’s attitude toward reform was molded by events. In his
letters as prince to Louis XVI, when speaking of reform, he men¬
tioned only the military changes necessary for the Ottoman '/
Empire to secure revenge from Russia and to regain the terri¬
tories lost to Catherine II. After he came to the throne in 1789,
his efforts went entirely into modernizing and reforming the
existing military corps, the Janissaries, the cavalry, and the
artillery. It must be granted that the danger of the war itself
made more comprehensive and radical reforms impossible. But
after the war was over, there was only one important change. In
addition to continuing his efforts to reform the old corps, or at
least those able and willing to accept such reforms, Selim also
responded to Janissary and cavalry military weakness and obdu¬
racy by introducing the Nizam-i Jedid army. But this was not
the new idea of nineteenth-century reform. Ottoman sultans had
been introducing new corps and new armies to make use of new
weapons and military techniques ever since the Janissary corps
had been specially created in the fifteenth century to use the
rifles, cannons, and gunpowder then introduced for the first time.
The Nizam-i Jedid army was no more than an enlarged and
modernized model of the rifle and cannon corps created during
the eighteenth century by Bonneval, Baron de Tott, and other
European advisors. So long as the establishment of the new army
was not accompanied by an effort to eliminate those members of




                   The Deposition of Mustafa IV
406   the afmy, government, and society who refused to accept reform
      and lived in the past, and so long as the Nizam-i Jedid and tech¬
      nical innovations were not in the context of the radical political,
      social, and economic reforms which made possible their develop¬
      ment and successful operation in the West, they cannot be consid¬
      ered as anything more than the last gasp of a dead tradition. One
      may argue that Selim would have gone on to such policies once
      his Nizam-i Jedid army was strong enough to overcome the
      resistance of the vested interests. Perhaps so, but during the
      entire eighteen years of his reign,^ Selim showed little evidence
      that he had intented to push on into these new fields or had the
      ability to do so.
        Selim was a ruler with good ideas but without the moral
      strength or the ability to put his ideas into practice. As soon as
      his limited military reforms aroused opposition, he modified
      them, he limited the size of the new army, he appointed conserva¬
      tives to key positions and he retired to the pleasures of the harem
      while leaving his reforming friends to fight their enemies. Instead
      of leading his supporters with an example of strength and deter¬
      mination, he sought their control by stimulating them to struggle
      for his favor, thus creating the same sort of political factionalism
      which had paralyzed Ottoman governments in the past.
        But as a man of his time, Selim did witness the introduction of
      new institutions, practices, and ideas into his empire, which
      necessarily began the process by which the old concept of reform
      was replaced by the new. The old tradition was molded by an
      Ottoman attitude which was largely isolated from the outside
      world, and which consequently assumed that the modern Otto¬
      man inferiority was due more to disruption of the older ways
      than it was to any new and more powerful institutions and prac¬
      tices developed in Europe. It was only when this Ottoman "iron
      curtain” of the past was broken down so that Ottomans could
      clearly see the tremendous political, economic, and social strength
      of the new Europe, that the old concept of reform was necessarily
      replaced by the new. And the events of the age of the French
      Revolution pierced this iron curtain in such a way that it never
      could be restored, no matter how many reformers were killed and
      institutions torn asunder. The incursions of European armies




                            The Triumph of Reaction
onto Ottoman soil, the arrival of large numbers of European         407
diplomats, soldiers, and merchants in the great cities of the
empire, the dispatch of numerous Ottomans to reside in the capi¬
tals of Europe, the blossoming of European society in Istanbul,
and the increased contacts between Ottomans and Europeans
accomplished this. Moreover even Selim’s limited military re¬
forms bore fruit far beyond their limited objectives. Men trained
in foreign languages and techniques for military purposes were
able to penetrate the great store of European literature and to
perceive more clearly the whole range of European life and
thought. The effectiveness of the new army, when contrasted
with the increasing inefficiency and anarchy of the Janissaries
and Spahis, provided a fitting lesson for all who could see. Al¬
though when the crisis came Selim betrayed the reformers to
their enemies in order to save himself, enough of them survived
and benefited from experience to nourish the seed and provide a
cadre of men able and willing to restore the reforms and move
beyond them as soon as the political situation made this possible
in the reign of Mahmud II.

                          I. Decline of the Ottoman Empire

          1. The decay of the Ottoman Empire is discussed by B. Lewis, "Some
      Reflections on the Decline of the Ottoman Empire,” Stadia Islamica, IX
      (1958), 111-127, and idem. The Emergence of Modern Turkey, 2nd ed.
      (London and New York, 1968), pp. 21-39. Contemporary Ottoman
      analyses of the situation include those oflKogi Bey, Kogi Bey Risalesi
      (Istanbul, 1277/1860, 1303/1886, 1939; , Paris, 1861; London, 1862);
      German trans. by W. F. Behrnauer^in ZDMG, XV (1861), 272-332;
      XVI (1862), 271-290; XVIII (1864), 699-740; French trans. by Petis de la
      Croix (Paris, 1725); Russian trans. by Vassily Dmitrievich Smirnov,
      Kotschybey (Saint Petersburg, 1873); Liitfl Pa§a, Asafname (Istanbul,
      1909; Berlin, 1910); San Mehmed Pa§a, Nasaih ul-vuzera vel-iimera,
      trans. by W. Wright as Ottoman Statecraft (Princeton, N. J., 1935);
      Haci Halife (Katib ^elebi), Dilstur iil-Amal li-Islah al-Halal (Istanbul,
      1280/1863); German trans. by W. F. Behrnauer in ZDMG, XI (1857),
      111-132. See also B. Lewis, "Ottoman Observers of Ottoman Decline,”
      Islamic Studies, I (1962), 71-87.
          2. The economic background of Ottoman decline is discussed in
      Ferdinand Braudel, La Mediterranee et le monde mediterraneen a I’epoque
      de Philippe II, 2nd ed., 2 vols. (Paris, 1966); and in a brilliant study by
      Halil Inalcik, "Osmanli Imparatorlugunun kurulu§ ve inkigafi devrinde
      Tiirkiyenin Iktisadi vaziyeti iizerinde bir tetkik miinasebetile,” Belleten,
      XV (1951), 629-684, with an English summary, "Remarks on an essay
      on the economical situation of Turkey,” on pp. 685-690. See also Mustafa
      Akdag, "Osmanb imparatorlugunun kurulu§ ve inkigafi devrinde
      Tiirkiye’nin iktisadi vaziyeti,” Belleten, XIII (1949), 497-571, XIV
      (1950), 319-418, an article which Inalcik shows must be used with
      considerable caution. On Ottoman internal disorder during this period,
      see the excellent contributions by Mustafa Akdag, "Celali Fetreti,”
      Ankara Universitesi DU ve Tarih-Cografya Fakultesi Dergisi, XVI (1958),
      53-107; idem, Celali Isyanlari, 1550-1603 (Ankara, 1963); and idem,
      Buyiik Celali Kari§ikliklarinin Ba§lamasi (Erzurum, 1963).
          3. On Murad IV’s reforms, see Ahmed Refik, "Sultan Murad-i Rabi’
      nin Hatt-i Hiimayunlari,” TOEM, III (1916), 129-141; Cavid Baysun,
      "Murad IV,” lA, VIII, 625-647. On the Kopriilii family, see Tayyib
      Gokbilgin, "Kopriiliiler,” lA, VI, 892-908; Paul Rycaut, The Present
      State of the Ottoman Empire, 2 vols. (Cologne, 1676); idem. The History
      of the Turkish Empire, 1623-1677, 3 vols. (London, 1680; Paris, 1683);
      also M. Brosch, Geschichten aus dem Leben dreier Grosswesire (Gotha,
      1899); and Petis de la Croix, Etat general de I’Empire Othoman (Paris,
      1695).

          40. In the traditional Ottoman military organization, the Cebeci



                               Notes to pages 122-125
corps performed most of the functions of a supply service for the fighting     433
corps. Its members were in charge of obtaining, storing, and supplying
ammunition, weapons, supplies, and food for the regular army, so its
barracks and headquarters, the Cehhane, was the Arsenal of the Otto¬
man army. As Ottoman military practices were modernized, each of the
fighting corps took over these functions for itself, so that by the start of
the nineteenth century the Cebeci corps had largely lost its old impor¬
tance and was little more than an anachronism, serving only as a means
of providing salaries and pensions to persons deserving rewards from the
State. Selim III made no effort to modernize it although there is evi¬
dence that he did plan to abolish it once his Nizam-i Cedid army was
strong enough to accomplish this. It was only in the reign of his suc¬
cessor that the idea of a modern, centralized supply corps was introduced,
a curious reversion''to traditional Ottoman practice. See Uzun5ar§ih,
Kapukulu, II, 3-31; and Mehmed Zeki Pakalin, Osmanli Tarih Deyim-
leri ve Terimleri Sozlugu, 3 vols. (Istanbul, 1946-1955), I, 263-264.

          57. BVA, Cevdet Maliye 2019; TKS, E 3967. Tax farms (Iltizam)
      were purchased at auctions (Mizad or Muzayede), at which those wishing
      to acquire them competed with each other, with the highest bidder being
      awarded the contract for the year. Ordinarily tax farm contracts were
      awarded only when the bidding pushed the sale price over an amount
      equal to five times the average annual profit (faiz) left to the previous
      tax farmer. When the Irad-i Cedid treasury took over an IItizam formerly
      farmed out by the regular treasury, it paid the latter the equivalent of
      this price. Once a tax farm was given to a tax farmer {Multezim), he was
      required to deliver a certain amount to the Treasury every year, and was
      allowed to keep the balance as profit for himself. The Irad-i Cedid treas¬
      ury now took over this function for the tax farms in question. See Stan¬
      ford J. Shaw, The Financial and Administrative Organization and
      Development of Ottoman Egypt (Princeton, N. J., 1962), pp. 34-40;
      Pakahn, II, 57-58; BVA Muhasebe 6094, fol. 128b.

     9. Ishak Bey’s career until Selim Ill’s accession is discussed in
Chapter II. After 1787, he maintained himself on a lavish scale in Paris
by securing money and other gifts from the French Foreign Minister
and the British and Russian ambassadors, promising each of them that
he would use his influence with the Sultan on their behalf. His dissolute
behavior and increasingly imprudent demands finally caused the French
government to encourage him to depart, and he left Marseilles in Feb¬
ruary 1790. But rather than going directly to Istanbul, he first landed
at the Dardanelles and then went to Izmir, where he waited to find out
whether or not his master had forgiven him. In the capital, the diplo¬
matic maneuvers of the various foreign ambassadors for the moment
concentrated on Ishak Bey, with the French striving to have him ad¬
mitted and the British and Swedish representatives trying to secure his
punishment and banishment in the fear that he would persuade Selim
to favor the French. In April 1790, he returned to Istanbul but was at
once banished to Lemnos, where he spent the next three years. Finally,
in the spring of 1794, he was pardoned and returned to Istanbul. But he

      ant to the Grand Admiral Kiichuk Huseyin Pasha, who became his
      guardian and protector. Thereafter Ishak acted mainly as French trans¬
      lator for the Grand Admiral and as a guide for foreigners who wished to
      visit the shipyard.

Austrian consulate, Ludolf, reported that the Ottoman fleet had 24 ships
of the line (including 5 under construction), 10 frigates, and 176 smaller
ships and boats, with 3,422 cannons and 30,000 men in all (HHS, Turkei-
II, 96). The anonymous Ottoman list made in 1800 and reprinted by
Karal described 45 newly built ships of the line, frigates, and corvettes
constructed between 1789 and 1800, with these ships alone having
22,245 men and officers and 2,376 cannons.
   In January 1806, Pierre Ruffin, then acting French ambassador in
Istanbul, reported that the Ottoman fleet had 20 ships of the line (with
between 118 and 50 cannons each), 20 frigates (between 30 and 48
cannon), and 14 corvettes (24 to 20 cannons), with an additional 5 ships
of the line under construction at Istanbul, Bodrum, Gemlik, Rhodes, and
Sinop (AE Turquie 211, fol. 51, 10 Jan. 1806). At the same time, the




                         Notes to pages 157-158
442   anonymous French official report "Essai sur la puissance navale des
      Turcs,” fols. 350-357, which was submitted in 1806 but presumably
      must have been based on information gathered in previous years,
      estimated that the Ottoman fleet had 120 ships in 1789, including 17
      ships of the line and 20 frigates and corvettes, and 25,000 sailors; 20
      ships of the line, 15 frigates, many small boats, and 25,000 sailors in
      1805; and 20 ships of the line, 15 frigates, 32 small boats, 2,156 cannons,
      and 40,000 sailors and seagoing soldiers in 1806. In January 1807, the
      British ambassador in Istanbul, James Arbuthnot, reported that the
      Ottomans had 9 ships of the line, 14 frigates, 10 corvettes, and some
      small ships anchored at Istanbul or vicinity, but that "there is hardly a
      man on board the ships who can be called a real seaman” (FO 78/55, no.
      10, 27 Jan. 1807), Cevdet^ (VII, 292-294) reported that in the year 1219/
      1804, the Ottoman fleet had 20 ships of the line, 22 frigates, 15 corvettes,
      totaling 61 warships in all. In 1803, the British ambassador in Istanbul,
      Drummond, reported to his government that the Ottoman fleet at that
      time was one of the "finest fleets” he ever saw (FO Turkey 40, 11 June
      1803).

          XIII. Administrative, Economic, and Social Reforms

     1. The power, status, and duties of every individual in the Ottoman
ruling class was determined by his rank and position, and was indicated
and defined as his Hadd, or "limit,” within which he was free to act
according to law and custom but beyond which he could not transgress.
To "violate the limits” of one’s own Hadd or that of another Ottoman was
considered a flagrant violation of the mores of Ottoman society and was
cause for severe punishment, in degrees up to the loss of position in the
Ottoman ruling class itself. Stanford J. Shaw, ed. and trans., Ottoman
Egypt in the Eighteenth Century (Cambridge, Mass., 1962), p. 23 n.
     2. See Avdo Suceska, "Bedeutung und Entwicklung des Begriffes
A'yan im Osmanischen Reich”. Sudost-Forschungen, XXV (1966), 3-26.
     3. Ottoman society was divided into a small group of slaves of the
Sultan who, as such, formed the Ottoman ruling class, and the mass of
subjects {reayd). The ruling class divided itself into a number of "institu¬
tions” to carry out its functions, and of these, the Imperial Institution,




                         Notes to pages 159-168
444   which managed the entire structure, gave the rank of vezir to its higher
      officials. The display of three horse-tails was allowed to publicly indicate
      this rank. See Pakahn, III, 590-593; Uzungar§ili, Merkez Te§kild,ti, pp.
      195-213.
           4. On the Mir-i Mirans and Beylerbeys, see V. L. Menage, "Begler-
      begi,” EP, I, 1159-1160; Gibb and Bowen, I/l, 137; Pakahn, I, 216-222.
           5. The laws reorganizing the corps of vezirs are given in full in
      Istanbul Municipal Library, MS Cevdet Yazmalar 032, fols. 25b-28a,
      and in Qavanin-i Sultan Selim, fols. 23a-26a; also Cavdet^, VI, 301-304;
      BVA, Maliyyeden Miidevvere 7584; they are summarized inUzun?ar§ili,

      Cevdet Yazmalar, 032, fol. 4a-b, dated 22 Ramadan 1206/14 May 1792.
      They are discussed in HHS, Tiirkei 11-103, no. 10 (12 April 1793).
           6. The Yillik-i Humayun (Annual Imperial Payment) was made by
      most high officials to the Sultan and members of his family once a year,
      usually at the start of the month of Ramazan. It was finally abolished in
      1836 by Mahmud II. Pakahn, III, 637.
